entry.title: 30 Days of Vibe Coding | Day 30: Series Recap and the Full Table of Contents
entry.content:
Intro

Somehow we've already made it to Day 30.

I'm keeping today simple: a few thoughts from me, and then everything organized into one table of contents.

Thoughts after 30 days

Hmm... honestly...

Non-technical writing is a real challenge for me. Explaining AI agents in particular was way harder than I expected, while just walking through a technology or a workflow felt pretty easy.

So Day 1 through Day 20 were relatively easy to write, but from Day 20 to Day 29 things got a lot harder (I may have even started slacking off a bit lol). If the second half feels kind of rough... please forgive me?!

Okay, enough rambling. Here's the table of contents, so you can find whatever you're looking for.

The full table of contents

I've grouped all 30 days by week. If something catches your eye, just click straight in:

Week 1: Getting the concepts and basics down

  • Day 1: The 30-Day Roadmap to Building an Expense Tracker App with Claude Code
  • Day 2: What Is Vibe Coding? A Different Kind of Knowing
  • Day 3: Installing Claude Code and Picking a Subscription Plan
  • Day 4: Your First Task — The Smallest Loop for Changing Code
  • Day 5: Permissions and Plan Mode — Stop Hitting Yes on Everything
  • Day 6: Context and Tokens — Why AI Gets Dumber the Longer You Chat
  • Day 7: Week 1 Wrap-Up — 5 Mistakes Beginners Make Most

Week 2: From one spec to a working MVP

  • Day 8: Turning Ideas into a Spec — Writing SPEC.md with AI
  • Day 9: Setting Up the Project with CLAUDE.md and git init
  • Day 10: Building the First Feature with Plan Mode
  • Day 11: One Feature at a Time — How to Split Your Prompts
  • Day 12: Something Broke?! A Debugging Workflow for Vibe Coding
  • Day 13: Bringing the Numbers to Life — A Stats Page and Pie Chart with Chart.js
  • Day 14: Week 2 Wrap-Up — Should You Actually Read AI-Written Code?

Week 3: Making the UI look good, then giving the AI some tools

  • Day 15: What Are Skills? Teaching AI How You Get Things Done
  • Day 16: Making the UI Look Good (Part 1) — The Frontend Design Plugin
  • Day 17: Making the UI Look Good (Part 2) — Locking In the Style with DESIGN.md
  • Day 18: Your First Skill — Writing SKILL.md from Scratch
  • Day 19: Subagents — Hiring a Code Review Sidekick
  • Day 20: MCP Basics — Make the AI Check the Latest Docs Before Answering
  • Day 21: Week 3 Wrap-Up — Skills, Subagents, or MCP? How to Choose

Week 4: Taking the project from "it works" to "ready to ship"

  • Day 22: Hooks — Claude Code's Lifecycle Triggers
  • Day 23: Tests as Your Safety Net — Unit Testing with Vitest
  • Day 24: Refactoring to Pay Down Tech Debt
  • Day 25: Going Live — Deploying to GitHub Pages
  • Day 26: Your First Update After Launch
  • Day 27: Pull Requests and Automatic Code Review with CodeRabbit
  • Day 28: Week 4 Wrap-Up — How to Save Tokens in Claude Code

The last two days

  • Day 29: My Vibe Coding Workflow SOP
  • Day 30: Series Recap and the Full Table of Contents

Wrapping up

That's about it. 30 days, and we're done.

To sum it all up:

  • A tiny app and a big project share the same skeleton: a spec, tests, reviews, and automated deployment.
  • Tools will keep changing, but describing, verifying, and breaking things down won't.
  • Your next step is to start a project of your own.

Thank you to everyone who made it this far, whether you built along every single day or just followed the story all the way to the finish line.

I'll keep writing about new pitfalls and new toys as standalone posts here on the blog.

I hope these 30 days helped you actually step into the world of Vibe Coding. That's a wrap, see you in the next series!

entry.title: 30 Days of Vibe Coding | Day 29: My Vibe Coding Workflow SOP
entry.content:
Intro

We're down to the second-to-last day, so let's look back over the whole development process, step by step!

Think of it as wrapping up the entire Vibe Coding series, so in the future you can just follow along without having to dig back through Day 1 to Day 28.

The six steps at a glance

Looking back over the earlier days, we've actually been repeating the same six steps all along:

  • Think it through
  • Lay the foundation
  • Plan first
  • Take small steps
  • Set up quality gates
  • Go live

Each stage has its own tools that fit it best, so I've put them in a table:

StepWhat you doWhat you use
1. Think it throughTalk the requirements into a spec and acceptance criteriaInterview-style prompts, SPEC.md
2. Lay the foundationWrite the shared understanding into filesgit, CLAUDE.md, DESIGN.md
3. Plan firstRead the plan before approving big changesPlan Mode, docs/plans
4. Take small stepsOne feature at a time: build, check, commitThe three parts of a prompt, /clear, the debugging trio
5. Set up quality gatesMake code quality automaticcode-reviewer, Hooks, tests, PRs, CodeRabbit
6. Go liveMerge into main and it deploys automaticallyGitHub Actions, GitHub Pages

Honestly, this is pretty much how real-world development works too.

Vibe Coding makes development really fast, but before you let the AI loose, every stage has a checkpoint: the spec catches the direction, Git catches mistakes, the plan catches the scope, checks and tests catch quality, and the deployment flow catches the launch. These checkpoints work like brakes. They're what let you drive fast with confidence.

One thing to keep in mind, though: these six steps aren't a straight line. They're a loop that keeps going. Every update after launch starts again from step one.

flowchart LR
    A["1 Think it through<br>spec and acceptance criteria"] --> B["2 Lay the foundation<br>git and docs"]
    B --> C["3 Plan first<br>Plan Mode"]
    C --> D["4 Take small steps<br>build, check, commit"]
    D --> E["5 Quality gates<br>Hooks, tests, reviews"]
    E --> F["6 Go live<br>merge into main, auto-deploy"]
    F -.->|"Next feature"| A

Hmm? Sounds a lot like Scrum (agile)? Yep, conceptually it's pretty similar. I've just broken each step down further and adjusted it for the way AI development works.

Agile is more of a philosophy (a set of values and principles), and Scrum is one framework for putting it into practice. These six steps are a process I put together myself, not something from any official docs.

Where did each step come from?

Next, of course, let's talk about where each step came from, so you can see this process wasn't pulled out of thin air. Every step exists because we fell into a hole first.

Step 1: Think it through

If you just tell the AI "make this page look better, you decide," the AI is basically just making it up as it goes.

So you end up saying over and over: no, not that, change it again, change it again. And now you're burning Tokens and time for nothing. It's like telling an engineer you want a system built without ever explaining what it's supposed to do. They have no choice but to fill in the gaps themselves.

So the way you use AI actually says a lot about how you usually communicate requirements to other people.

Step 2: Lay the foundation

Once the requirements are talked through, it's time to lay the foundation. Here, the foundation is:

  • Git: lets you go back to an earlier save point.
  • CLAUDE.md: write down the principles you and the AI agreed on, so it reads them in every new conversation.
  • DESIGN.md: write down what the screens look like, so it reads that in every new conversation.
  • SPEC.md: write down the requirements, so it reads them in every new conversation.

One thing to watch out for, though: when Claude Code starts a new conversation, it only reads CLAUDE.md automatically. So DESIGN.md and SPEC.md have to be pulled in from CLAUDE.md with @ (for example, a line that says @SPEC.md) for the AI to read them too.

This is also the stage where you settle on the tech you'll use. Don't just go with whatever tech the AI suggests. Ask it about the pros and cons first, and then you make the call.

Step 3: Plan first

So next, do we just start building straight from the requirements in SPEC.md?

Nope. Don't forget the AI has its limits. Especially with big changes, it might miss some details or build something you didn't want.

So you should first have it write up a plan that lists which files it'll touch, what it won't do, and what the acceptance criteria are, and then you review it.

And have it save these Plan Mode plans in docs/plans/. Later, when a bug shows up, you can pull them out and check whether it actually followed the plan, or even use them to prove yourself wrong you're the one who said to do it this way, and then you blamed the AI for getting it wrong.

Step 4: Take small steps

Once the plan checks out, you can start building, of course. But here I'd recommend doing just one feature at a time.

Why? Say you eat three things you've never tried before and break out in hives. You'd have no idea which one caused it. It's the same with AI: if you ask it to change N features at once, when something breaks, you have no idea which change broke it.

So each round goes like this:

  • /clear first to wipe the last round's conversation and get a clean desk.
  • Ask the AI to build just one feature.
  • Check it yourself by hand, and only commit once it passes.

When you're checking, pay special attention to this: passing your checks doesn't mean there are no bugs. It might just mean you didn't happen to test that scenario. So put a few risky cases into your acceptance criteria on purpose, like data that crosses dates, last month's data, or an amount that exactly equals the budget. And click around the old features while you're at it, to make sure this change didn't break them.

If something really does break, don't worry. But never just say "it's broken, fix it" and send the AI off to change things. That's like going to the doctor and only saying "I don't feel well." The doctor can only guess. You have to describe clearly what's broken:

  1. How to reproduce it
  2. What you expected to see
  3. What you actually saw

That's basically a fixed debugging SOP.

If a few rounds back and forth still don't fix it, try asking from a different angle or narrowing down the scope. If that still doesn't work, use git to restore the broken files, go back to the last save point, and start over.

Step 5: Set up quality gates

The feature's done, so what keeps the quality up? Are you supposed to check everything yourself?

No way. People forget things, let alone AI. If you tell a coworker "remember to turn off the AC" every day before leaving, they'll remember most of the time, but there'll always be that one day they forget. A Hook is like setting the AC on a shutoff timer: when the time comes, it turns off, guaranteed.

So for things you need to check every time, like formatting and tests, don't just write them in CLAUDE.md and beg the AI to remember. Hand them to a Hook, so they run automatically the moment the time comes.

That doesn't mean you can skip checking things yourself, though. You still need to click through every new feature by hand once. It's just that the checks you'd repeat every single time get handed over to a mechanism. After all, with Vibe Coding you're not really reading the AI's code line by line, so something needs to keep an eye on the parts you don't see.

I split the gates into these:

  • Hooks: things that have to happen every time, like auto-formatting after the AI edits a file, or running the tests automatically after each round.
  • Tests: let the code check itself. Turn the acceptance criteria in SPEC.md into tests, especially for things like money calculations, where getting it wrong causes real trouble.
  • code-reviewer: a look-but-don't-touch subagent that reviews the AI's code with a fresh pair of eyes.
  • PRs: once you open a PR, GitHub Actions (GitHub's service that runs commands for you automatically) runs the tests and build, and CodeRabbit (an AI service that does code review for you automatically) reviews it one more time.

Pay special attention here: code-reviewer is a bit different from the other gates. It doesn't run on its own. It only goes to work when you call it. And sometimes the main agent decides it can just do the review itself (stubborn), and never hands it off at all. So after a feature is done, it's best to call it out directly with @, which guarantees it actually gets the job.

So why open a PR instead of pushing straight to main? Because every push to main deploys automatically, which means it goes live for everyone to see right away. So normally you branch off develop to do the work, then open a PR asking to merge back into develop when you're done. Think of a PR as a request form: you only hit merge after all the gates have run and you've looked at the results.

Also, just because a mechanism is set up doesn't mean it's running the way you think.

It's like installing a smoke detector at home but never pressing the test button, and then only finding out the battery died ages ago when there's an actual fire.

Take our formatting Hook. The files looked perfectly tidy, but it turned out later that Prettier had no config file at all. It had been formatting with its own defaults the whole time, so the quotes and semicolons didn't match the way the project was originally written. And since this kind of problem doesn't break any features, nobody noticed.

So after you set up a gate, remember to go back once and check that it's actually following the rules you want. Same goes for tests and GitHub Actions: break the code on purpose once and see whether it goes red, then change it back once you've confirmed it catches the problem. After all, if you've never seen it catch an error with your own eyes, how do you know it hasn't just been waving everything through?

And when it really does go red, don't panic. Don't merge yet. Paste the error message to the AI, have it fix things, then push to the same branch and let it run again.

As for the reports from code-reviewer and CodeRabbit, you do need to read them, but you don't have to fix everything. Handle the more serious ones first (like what CodeRabbit marks as high or medium), and talk the low ones over with the AI to see whether they really need fixing. The severity the AI assigns is just its opinion, not a royal decree. Whether to change something is still your call.

Step 6: Go live

All the gates have passed, so you can finally go live. But all-green Actions doesn't mean your site is fine.

It's like a food delivery app saying "Delivered." That doesn't mean the food is actually in your hands. Maybe it got left on the wrong floor. You still have to open the door and look.

What I mean is, all-green Actions only tells you the deployment process finished. For example, when you deploy to GitHub Pages, the URL gets an extra layer with the project name (like /money-note/). If vite.config.js doesn't set base, you'll open it to a blank white screen, and Actions will still be all green. So it only counts once you've opened the live URL and clicked around yourself.

Also, once you're on the PR workflow, the moment you merge develop into main is the moment you go live. So all those gates have to pass before you hit merge.

If it's your first time making a project public, then before you push, have the AI check the commit history for keys, passwords, .env files, and anything else that shouldn't be public. Once it's pushed, even if you delete the file afterward, it's still visible in the commit history.

And then back to step one

After launch, whether you're building the next feature or changing an old one, you start again from step one. And remember one big rule:

Update the rule docs first, then start building.

Why? Because in every new conversation, the AI works off docs like SPEC.md and CLAUDE.md. It's like a contractor building from blueprints: if you want to change the floor plan but don't update the blueprints, of course they'll keep building the old version.

Take our budget alerts. When we deliberately stuffed them into the plan early on, the "Out" list in SPEC.md blocked them. Later, when we actually wanted to build the feature, we went back to step one and updated the spec first, and that's how it got built smoothly.

As for what to build in the next loop, you don't have to come up with it out of nowhere. The docs/TODO.md you saved while taking stock of tech debt is a ready-made list of candidates. Just pick the smallest, lowest-risk one and start there.

When you run into new holes in the future, please write them into the process too, so the process remembers what it cost you instead of relying on your own memory. As for where to write them, use the split we covered earlier: what to build goes in SPEC.md, what the screens look like goes in DESIGN.md, principles that take judgment go in CLAUDE.md, things that must happen every time go to a Hook, anything you've said three or more times becomes a Skill, and logic that causes trouble when it's wrong gets tests.

Slim the steps down, but don't skip them

At this point you might be thinking: going through all six steps just to change a button's color? That's exhausting.

Actually, how much each step involves can scale with the size of the feature. For a small feature like budget alerts, the interview only took around eight questions to get aligned, and the plan got approved as soon as the scope looked reasonable. The official best practices say something similar: if you can describe the change in one sentence, you don't need to plan first.

So how big counts as a big change? My own rule: if it'll touch two or more files, it's a project I'm not familiar with, or I don't really have a clear idea myself, I turn on Plan Mode first.

But slimming down and skipping are two different things. It's like heading out the door: you don't drag a suitcase along to grab breakfast at the corner, but you take your keys and phone no matter where you go. Acceptance criteria are those keys. No feature is too small for them, because the step you skip thinking you'll get away with it is usually the exact step that blows up later (don't ask me how I know).

SOP checklist for your next project

Here I've boiled the six steps down into one checklist. On your next project, go through it line by line for every feature you build:

  • Think it through: Can you say what you should see when it's done? Does SPEC.md cover what you'll build, what you won't, and the acceptance criteria?
  • Lay the foundation: Is git clean before you start? Are the decisions you agreed on all written into SPEC.md, CLAUDE.md, or DESIGN.md?
  • Plan first: Will it touch two or more files, is it an unfamiliar project, or do you not really have a clear idea yet? If so, read the plan first: which files it touches, what it won't do, and how it'll be checked.
  • Take small steps: Is this round just one feature? Did you check it by hand, including the risky cases and the old features, before committing?
  • Quality gates: Is npm test green? Did you call code-reviewer with @ to review it? Did you branch off develop, open a PR, and look at the Actions and CodeRabbit results?
  • Go live: After merging into main, did you open the live URL and click through it yourself?

Yep, that's it. Just these six.

Wrapping up

We're about at the end, so here's a quick summary:

  • My Vibe Coding workflow is: think it through, lay the foundation, plan first, take small steps, set up quality gates, go live, and then back to step one.
  • Every step exists because we fell into a hole first. When you hit new ones, write them into the process.
  • You can slim the steps down, but don't skip them. Acceptance criteria are never optional.
  • Processes you keep repeating can be turned into Skills and handed to the AI, but checking the work and deciding whether to merge and go live are still up to you.
  • Keep the resource list handy, and when you hit a technical question, always check the official docs first.

Tomorrow's the last day. I'll put all 30 posts into one table of contents, so it's easier to come back and look things up later.

I hope this post helps you take what we did over these 30 days with you.

See you tomorrow!

entry.title: 30 Days of Vibe Coding | Day 28: Week 4 Wrap-Up — How to Save Tokens in Claude Code
entry.content:
Intro

Well... we've made it to Week 4, the final week, which also makes this the last wrap-up of the whole series.

For this wrap-up, let's talk about usage limits.

If you've been Vibe Coding along this whole time, you've probably run into the usage limit more than a few times by now. So this post is all about that.

Quick bit of background first: on the Pro and Max plans, your usage is shared between chatting on claude.ai and Claude Code. And there are two kinds of limits: a five-hour session limit and a weekly limit.

First, how does your usage get eaten up?

After everything we've covered, I'm sure you know by now that the biggest catch with AI is the Token limit, and how many Tokens you burn mainly comes down to the size of the "Context."

The key point fits in one sentence:

Context is everything on the table. The more stuff there is, the more Tokens each round uses, and the more it costs.

Most of the Context gets taken up by these:

  • Chat history: This is the big one. Remember the table I used as an example back on Day 6? Basically, every time the AI replies to you, it has to look over the entire Context Window (the tabletop) again, so the longer you chat, the more Tokens you spend.
  • Files it reads and command output: Every file the AI reads and every npm test it runs, all that content and those results go into the Context, and they get read again on the next round.
  • CLAUDE.md: It's loaded automatically every time you start a new conversation, including the file we pulled in with @DESIGN.md on Day 17. So the fatter it gets, the more every round costs. The official docs also recommend keeping CLAUDE.md under 200 lines.
  • Skills: From my teaching experience, a lot of Vibe Coding beginners tend to install a whole pile of Skills. But every installed Skill keeps its description sitting on the table the whole time, and the body of any Skill that's been called stays in the conversation until you /clear.
  • MCP: MCP tool names are always on the table, but that part's pretty small. What really takes up space is after one gets triggered, when MCP dumps whatever it found into the Context.
  • Subagents: As we covered on Day 19, a subagent has its own Context Window, so it doesn't get mixed into your main conversation. But every subagent you spin up still has its Context counted toward your usage.

So you'll notice a lot of Token usage happens without you even realizing it. You might just want to look something up in the docs, run a test, or add a Skill, and before you know it the table's gotten pretty bloated.

That's also why I suggested right from the start that you begin with the $20 subscription. That's how you find out how much usage you actually need, without wasting a bunch of money.

So how do you save?

It's actually pretty simple. Just stick to a few big principles:

  • The smaller the Context, the less you spend: /clear when you're done. Don't leave everything sitting on the table.
  • Don't pile on external tools (MCP, Skills): If you don't need an external tool, don't install it. They stay on the table eating Context the whole time. It might not be much, but if one gets triggered by accident, it can eat a ton.
  • Redoing work costs the most: For big changes, run Plan Mode first. Heading in the wrong direction and having to redo everything is the most expensive thing there is.

Fun fact: someone on the Claude Code team once said publicly that AI is smart enough now that you don't really need to lean on Plan Mode anymore (though they also said Plan Mode isn't going away). Still, I think it's really useful, because it lets you check the direction before a big change and avoid redoing work.

Week 4 hands-on checklist

Same as the first three weeks, here's a checklist for the wrap-up. Go through it line by line and see whether you've actually done each one:

  • The project has at least one Hook set up (Day 22)
  • The core money-calculation logic has tests, and you've made them fail and then pass again (Day 23)
  • Used Plan Mode to take stock of all the tech debt (Day 24)
  • Did one post-launch update, changing SPEC first before touching anything (Day 26)
  • Every addition and edit branches off develop, goes through a PR, and you've fixed things based on CodeRabbit's suggestions (Day 27)
  • Tried /usage to check your usage, and /context to see what's on the table

Wrapping up

We're about at the end, so here's a quick summary:

  • Pro and Max usage is shared between claude.ai chat and Claude Code, and the limits come in two kinds: a five-hour session limit and a weekly limit.
  • Token usage mainly comes down to the size of the Context. Chat history, files it reads and command output, CLAUDE.md, Skills, MCP, and subagents all eat into your usage, and a lot of it happens without you noticing.
  • Saving usage comes down to three principles: /clear when you're done to keep the Context as small as possible, don't pile on MCP servers and Skills you don't use, and run Plan Mode before big changes so you don't have to redo work.
  • Start with the $20 plan, get a feel for how much usage you really need, then decide whether to upgrade.

That wraps up all four full weeks. Tomorrow we'll turn everything we've done over these 30 days into an SOP, along with a resource list worth bookmarking.

I hope this post helps you spend your usage where it actually counts. See you tomorrow!

entry.title: 30 Days of Vibe Coding | Day 27: Pull Requests and Automatic Code Review with CodeRabbit
entry.content:
Intro

Yesterday we did a quick review: we moved the "budget alerts" feature off the original "Out" list, made a plan with Plan Mode, built it, and finally pushed to main so GitHub Actions deployed it automatically.

But next I want to talk about a more proper development workflow: the PR (Pull Request) workflow.

In short, before our code lands on main and gets deployed, the changes go through a few checks first so we don't break the live site. And the whole thing is automatic.

What's a PR?

Back on Day 25 I briefly mentioned branches. I said you didn't need to understand them yet, but now it's time to actually spend a bit of time on them.

First off, in a proper development workflow, we keep production and development separate:

  • Production: This is the main branch. Every push to it deploys automatically to the live URL, which is the public-facing environment. So once something's out there, real users are seeing it.
  • Development: This is the develop branch. It doesn't deploy to the live URL. It's mainly where developers test, check their work, and fix bugs.
  • Branch: A copy, or draft, split off from main or develop. You can make changes on this draft, test them, and check them without affecting main or develop. Common ones are feature branches, bugfix branches, hotfix branches, and so on.

So starting today, the expense tracker app follows this flow too. Every time we change anything, we branch off develop, merge back into develop when we're done, test it in the test environment, and once everything checks out, merge develop into main to go live.

So... what's a PR (Pull Request)?

Basically, think of it as a request form. It says: "I'd like to merge this draft (the feature branch) into develop" (or "merge develop into main"). And that request form can come with a few checks, like:

  • Automated tests: did this change break anything that used to work?
  • AI review: does this change have any security concerns or code quality problems?
  • Human review: does this change follow the team's conventions, and is the code style okay?

That's the process we're adding here. Once it's in place, the whole thing looks like this:

flowchart TB
    subgraph G1["Feature branch → develop"]
        direction LR
        A["Branch off develop<br>make changes on the branch"] --> B["Open a PR<br>to develop"]
        B --> C["Automatic checks<br>merge only if they pass"]
    end
    subgraph G2["develop → main"]
        direction LR
        D["Confirm develop<br>is all good"] --> E["Open a PR<br>to main"]
        E --> F["Automatic checks<br>merge only if they pass"]
    end
    G1 --> G2
    G2 --> H["main updates<br>auto-deploys live"]

With the basics down, we're going to bring in an AI code review service called CodeRabbit, so every PR gets reviewed automatically the moment it opens, with comments left in Chinese (or whatever language you set).

CodeRabbit

So what's this CodeRabbit I keep mentioning? In short, it's an AI code review service. Once you install it on your GitHub repository, whenever certain PRs get opened, CodeRabbit automatically reviews the changes and leaves comments right on the PR.

So... an AI code review service can't be completely free, right? After all, we've said over and over that the most expensive part of AI is compute.

And you'd be right. CodeRabbit has paid plans, billed monthly per developer. The Essentials plan is $30 per person per month ($24 if you pay annually).

But it's really generous with public repositories. If your repo is public, you can use PR code review for free once it's installed, no credit card needed. On the other hand, for a private repo the free plan only gives you PR summaries. The real line-by-line review is paid.

Conveniently, our money-note project is public, so we can demo it right away.

A lot of services build their free plans around open source projects, because open source gives back to the community. That's part of why we went with a public repository for this project. The users these companies actually make money from are private repositories on paid plans, since those are usually for commercial use. That's where the value is for them, and those users are more willing to pay.

So why do we still need CodeRabbit when we already set up code-reviewer back on Day 19?

Because code-reviewer only does anything when you call it, while CodeRabbit lives on GitHub and runs automatically whenever you open a PR. Put that together with the Hooks and CLAUDE.md we learned earlier, and the full development flow ends up looking like this:

flowchart TB
    subgraph L["Local (Claude Code)"]
        direction TB
        A["AI follows the CLAUDE.md rules<br>and edits code on a feature branch"] --> B["PostToolUse Hook<br>auto-formats with Prettier"]
        B --> C["npm test<br>runs tests locally"]
        C -.->|"call it yourself when needed"| D["code-reviewer<br>local review"]
        C --> E["commit<br>push the feature branch"]
        D -.-> E
    end
    subgraph G["GitHub"]
        direction TB
        F["Open a PR<br>feature → develop"] --> H["GitHub Actions runs tests<br>CodeRabbit reviews automatically"]
        H --> I["Merge into develop"]
        I --> J["Open a PR<br>develop → main"]
        J --> K["GitHub Actions runs tests<br>CodeRabbit reviews automatically"]
        K --> M["Merge into main"]
        M --> N["deploy.yml auto-deploys<br>live on GitHub Pages"]
    end
    E --> F

You can see review shows up all through our flow, from code-reviewer on your machine to CodeRabbit on GitHub, so every single change gets checked.

So after all that talk, what do we actually do? It's simple:

  1. Open the CodeRabbit website, click Log In, then click Login with GitHub, and hit Authorize coderabbitai.
  2. Pick which account to install it on. Here, choose your own GitHub account.
  3. Click Install & Authorize and you're done.

Have the AI add the config

What's next? Let's try opening a PR and see whether CodeRabbit reviews it automatically.

Before that, though, there's some setup to do: adding a config file called .coderabbit.yaml to the project. This file mainly sets CodeRabbit's review language, which branches to review, and so on.

Same as always, just hand it to the AI. Type /clear to clear the conversation, then enter this prompt:

I want to add a PR workflow to this project. main is production and develop is development. Please do four things:

1. Add .github/workflows/test.yml so that whenever there's a PR to merge into develop or main, it automatically runs npm ci, npm test, and npm run build.
2. Add .coderabbit.yaml, set the review language to zh-TW, and make PRs that merge into develop get reviewed automatically too.
3. Add rules to CLAUDE.md: from now on, every change branches off develop, pushes the branch, and opens a PR to merge back into develop; when it's time to go live, open a develop → main PR; never push directly to develop or main.
4. When all of that is done, commit and push to main. This is the last direct push. Then create a develop branch from main and push it.

Now we can try creating a PR.

The first PR

CodeRabbit's ready, so of course we want to trigger it. Type /clear to clear the conversation, then enter this prompt:

Please pick the smallest, lowest-risk item from docs/TODO.md and build it.

While building, make sure to follow the new rules in CLAUDE.md: create a new branch off develop, run npm test when you're done, commit, then push this branch. Don't touch develop or main.

Once it's pushed, go back to your repo page on GitHub and create a PR. Wait a moment, and you'll see the tests and CodeRabbit's review kick off automatically, with comments showing up on the PR.

Here's an example PR for reference: example PR

On top of that, GitHub itself offers an extra free code review option. Just add Copilot in the Reviewers field next to the PR, and Copilot will review your code too.

Try it: what do you do when Actions goes red?

So... everything so far has basically been a demo of things going right, which makes it hard to tell whether any of this actually works.

So I'm leaving you a little homework: go back and trigger some of these Actions failures yourself.

Just ask the AI to remove the $ from what formatAmount outputs on a branch, then push without running the tests, and you'll see Actions fail. I won't demo this part. I'll leave it for you to try at home.

What do you do with CodeRabbit's comments?

The tests are covered. So what about all those comments CodeRabbit left?

Here's the big-picture rule: CodeRabbit labels its suggestions high, medium, or low. Focus mainly on high and medium. For the low ones, talk them over with the AI and see whether they really need fixing.

Because sometimes AI is a little too sensitive. Say you've got a console.log in your code. CodeRabbit might suggest removing it, but maybe that console.log is something you need while testing. In that case you can just ignore it.

So how do you get the AI to fix CodeRabbit's suggestions? A couple of ways:

  • Manually copy the CodeRabbit comment, paste it to the AI, and ask it to fix it.
  • Have the AI go read CodeRabbit's comments directly, which you'll need the Claude in Chrome extension for.

Personally, I use the second one more often.

Wrapping up

That's about it for this one, so let's sum up:

  • Keep production (main) and development (develop) separate. Every change branches off develop, merges back into develop first, and only after you've confirmed it's fine does develop get merged into main to go live.
  • A PR is a request form. Before any change gets into develop or main, it has to pass checks like automated tests and AI review.
  • CodeRabbit is free for public repositories, and because it lives on GitHub, it reviews automatically whenever you open a PR. Unlike code-reviewer, you don't have to remember to call it.
  • Besides CodeRabbit, you can also add Copilot under Reviewers on a GitHub PR, so one more AI looks over your code.
  • You don't have to fix every one of CodeRabbit's suggestions. Focus on the high and medium ones, and talk the low ones over with the AI to see whether they really need fixing.

And don't forget the homework: make Actions go red once with your own hands.

entry.title: 30 Days of Vibe Coding | Day 26: Your First Update After Launch
entry.content:
Intro

Once a system goes live, does it stop changing?

Nope, you've got that wrong.

After launch, a system actually changes even more, since you'll need to adjust to what users want, how the market shifts, what competitors do, and even changes in regulations.

So in the world of Vibe Coding, how do you add a new feature after launch?

That's what this post is about.

Update the spec before you touch anything

If you remember, on Day 10 we did a scope-control exercise. We deliberately threw in a line asking for budget alerts and income tracking, and the AI pulled out the "Out" list in SPEC.md and blocked the request.

So... now that the system is live, what if you actually want that feature? It's pretty simple. Whenever you start expanding requirements, stick to one big rule:

Update the rule docs first, then start building.

Never, ever change the code first. It's a really bad habit. It's easy for the docs to fall behind the code, then you can't check features against them anymore, and every update after that just piles more on top of a shaky foundation.

So what should we do now? Pretty simple. Go into Claude Code, type /clear to wipe the conversation (so the Context is clean), and then enter this prompt:

Please read @SPEC.md. There's a "### Out (explicitly excluded from v1)" list in it, and I want you to move "Budgets and over-budget alerts" off that list.
I'm about to build the "Budgets and over-budget alerts" feature, so after you move it, switch into the role of a "product consultant."
Interview me about this feature, asking one question at a time, to pin down the requirements.
Once you think it's specific enough, tell me it's ready to be written into SPEC.md, and ask me to confirm.

At this point you might be wondering: should we switch to Plan Mode for this?

Let's do a quick review:

  • Plan Mode: It's geared toward getting to work once the plan is done. It produces an implementation plan (which files to touch, what the steps are), then asks whether you want it to go ahead. It'll still ask you questions when something's unclear, but those questions are all about what it needs "to lock down the plan and start building."
  • Interview-style prompt: It's geared toward clarifying requirements. The goal isn't to start building, so what it mainly produces is a requirements spec. You only need to figure out the what (what to build) for now. The how (how to build it) is Plan Mode's job later. And you're the one controlling the pace of the questions, since you told it to dig one question at a time, instead of letting it decide on its own when it's asked enough.

To simplify it even more:

  • The interview asks the what (what to build)
  • Plan Mode asks the how (how to build it)

Right now we haven't even figured out what the budget looks like or how the over-budget alert should be displayed, so this isn't the time for Plan Mode. Plan Mode would just rush to lay out implementation steps for you, while the requirements aren't even lined up yet. So here you only need to switch to manual mode on, and then get ready to be grilled one question at a time.

In my case, I got grilled with at least 8 or so questions (it'll be different for everyone).

Building the feature with Plan Mode

What's next? It's pretty straightforward from here, and it's about the same as what we've done before. Just switch to Plan Mode and enter this prompt:

Please build the budget alert feature following the updated @SPEC.md.

If the plan looks fine, let the AI build it. Once it's done, you still need to do some review. You can come up with some edge cases to check, like:

  1. Get this month's total to exactly 1000 on purpose and set the budget to 1000. At this point, there shouldn't be an alert.
  2. Add another $1, and it should show you're $1 over.
  3. Refresh the page, and the budget and the alert are both still there.
  4. Clear the budget to 0, and the alert goes away.

You can hand the edge cases above to the AI and have it use the Claude in Chrome extension to drive the screen and test them itself.

After that it gets a lot easier. Just ask the AI to push it live, since we already set up GitHub Actions auto-deployment on Day 25.

Wrapping up

This one was a lot simpler, since most of it was already covered in earlier days. So today was mostly a review, so you know what to do when you want to add a new feature after launch.

Here's a quick recap:

  • To add a new feature after launch, update the spec before you touch anything. Never change the code first.
  • Use an interview-style prompt to ask the what and clarify the requirements, and only go into Plan Mode to ask the how once the requirements are lined up. Don't mix the two up.
  • For small features, the interview and the plan can both be small, but don't skip the acceptance criteria. Before you start building, think through a few edge cases first.

That's it for this one. See you tomorrow!

entry.title: 30 Days of Vibe Coding | Day 25: Going Live — Deploying to GitHub Pages
entry.content:
Intro

"If nobody else can see it, you're just impressing yourself."

Yep. No matter how useful the project you've been building is, it still only lives at localhost:5173, an address that only your own computer knows about.

So today I'm going to show you how to use GitHub Pages to put your project out there, so other people can see it and actually use it.

Why GitHub Pages?

I'm guessing a lot of people's first reaction is: "Why GitHub Pages?"

It's pretty simple. Our project is a front-end project — no back end, no database, no login — so anywhere that can host static files will work.

And there are three reasons I picked GitHub Pages:

  1. All you need is a GitHub account, so there's no extra service to sign up for.
  2. GitHub Pages gives you roughly 100GB of bandwidth a month, which is plenty for a small project.
  3. GitHub Actions can automate deployment. After you push, it builds, uploads, and deploys on its own, so you skip the hassle of uploading by hand.

Overall, you don't need to spend extra time learning Cloudflare Pages or Vercel. GitHub alone covers everything we need.

You're also going to see the word "build" a lot in a minute. In short, it means packaging our app into a bundle of purely static files (HTML, CSS, JS). The packaged files go into a folder called dist/, and "deploying" really just means putting that folder on GitHub Pages.

So here's what the flow will look like once it's running:

flowchart LR
    A["git push"] --> B["GitHub Actions starts"]
    B --> C["npm test<br>npm run build"]
    C --> D["Hand dist to GitHub Pages"]
    D --> E["Public URL updates automatically"]

Then you get a public URL just for this project, something like https://your-username.github.io/repo-name/, and you can share it with anyone!

You basically only have to set this up once. After that, every push to the main branch deploys automatically.

GitHub is a third-party code hosting platform. Its Pages feature is free, but it isn't built specifically for hosting websites. If your project is commercial or gets a lot of traffic, I'd recommend finding a service made for that. This post is only meant for practice or personal projects.

Wait, didn't we say no GitHub Pages?

If you remember, back on Day 9 we didn't specifically say to use GitHub Pages. We let the AI make that call for us.

Don't believe me? In my case, if I open CLAUDE.md, there's a section that says:

## Deployment

The build output is purely static files, targeting Cloudflare Pages or Vercel, so **there's no need to set `base` in `vite.config.js`**. It's only needed if we switch to GitHub Pages (monorepo subpath), but TECH_CHOICE.md already decided not to go that route.

Everyone's AI writes slightly different things, so it's totally normal if your CLAUDE.md and TECH_CHOICE.md don't mention this.

So this is the perfect moment to change that decision. In real projects, requirements change out of nowhere all the time. Open Claude Code again, type /clear to wipe the conversation, and then enter this prompt:

Switch deployment to GitHub Pages instead of Cloudflare Pages / Vercel.

Please add a row to the decision log in section 10 of SPEC.md (date, decision, reason).

Also update the deployment sections in CLAUDE.md and TECH_CHOICE.md so they all match.

Yep, it's that simple. The AI updates all three files for you. That's the power of Vibe Coding.

But notice we still haven't started building anything, because we want to line up the docs first. That way we won't end up with "the docs say one thing and the code does another."

Pushing the project to GitHub

Next, there's something I need you to check first: if you don't have a GitHub account yet, go sign up for one.

Once you're signed up, go to the GitHub home page, click + in the top right → New repository, and enter a Repository name (I'd suggest money-note, same as the project name). Leave every other option unchecked, then click Create repository.

Below that, you'll see a bunch of commands:

git remote add origin git@github.com:hsiangfeng/money-note.git
git branch -M main
git push -u origin main

Copy those commands and paste them into the prompt below so the AI can take care of it for you (remember to swap in the commands GitHub gave you — don't copy mine):

I've already created a new repo on GitHub. Here are the commands GitHub gave me:

git remote add origin git@github.com:hsiangfeng/money-note.git
git branch -M main
git push -u origin main

After adding the remote, please don't push right away. First check the current commit history and files for anything that shouldn't be public: keys, passwords, .env, personal data. Also run `npm test`, `npm run build`, and `git status`, and only push once everything checks out.

You might be wondering why I don't just push the whole project up in one go. It's because we want to check the commit history for anything that shouldn't be public first, and have the AI run a few checks while it's at it:

Once you've fixed whatever needs fixing, head back to your repo page on GitHub and you'll see the project is up there!

Auto-deploying with GitHub Actions

So is that it? Are we done?

Nope. So far we've only "hosted" the code on GitHub. It isn't actually deployed to GitHub Pages yet.

So once the project's pushed, we'll ask the AI to set up a GitHub Actions workflow that handles deployment for us automatically.

In normal development, we split work into branches — a development branch, a testing branch, a production branch, and so on. In most real projects, only the Main branch (or Master branch) gets deployed to production, and the other branches are for testing environments.

What about us? Do we need that? Not yet, unless you're really curious about it. So we'll just stick with the default branch (Main): push to Main, and it deploys automatically.

All you need to do is tell the AI this:

Add automatic deployment to GitHub Pages. This step only adds .github/workflows/deploy.yml:

- Trigger on push to main
- Use the latest Node LTS, and run npm ci, npm test, npm run build first
- Use GitHub's official Pages actions to upload dist and deploy

Normally, if your AI is smart enough (lol), it should catch a gotcha:

This base: '/money-note/' gotcha is the one beginners hit most often, because GitHub Pages URLs usually look like this:

https://your-username.github.io/repo-name/

So if you don't set base, you're guaranteed to get a white screen. After the build, all the CSS, JS, images, and so on in your code get looked up starting from the root path /, and that's how you end up with a blank white page.

So if you run into this, adding base: '/repo-name/' to vite.config.js fixes it.

There's one more thing to adjust before you push, though. Go to your GitHub repo → Settings → Pages → Build and deployment → Source, and pick GitHub Actions. New repositories don't have Pages turned on by default, so if you skip this, Actions will throw an error in a minute.

If everything looks fine so far, ask the AI to commit the current progress and push it to GitHub, and you'll see Actions start running.

If Actions throws an error along the way, it's almost always because you forgot to change the Pages Source in your repo. Go back, fix that setting, and push again.

If everything went smoothly, your project is now officially live for the world to see!

Here's my demo URL for reference: https://israynotarray.com/money-note/

Since I use a custom domain, my URL doesn't look like https://your-username.github.io/repo-name/.

Wrapping up

We're about out of time, so here's a final recap:

  • Deploying really just means building the app into static files (dist/) and putting them on GitHub Pages. GitHub Actions automates that for you: set it up once, and every push to main deploys automatically.
  • Even though the original plan was to skip GitHub Pages, when you change a decision, update the related docs to match so the code and the docs don't drift apart.
  • Before you push the project to a public repo, have the AI check the commit history and files for anything that shouldn't be public, and run npm test and npm run build once too.
  • GitHub Pages URLs have an extra /repo-name/ layer, so remember to set base in vite.config.js. Without it, you'll get a white screen.
  • Before you push, go to Settings → Pages and set Source to GitHub Actions, or Actions will throw an error.

Hope this post got you the public URL you wanted for your project!

entry.title: 30 Days of Vibe Coding | Day 24: Refactoring to Pay Down Tech Debt
entry.content:
Intro

Wait... AI-written code can have tech debt too?

Of course! Even AI racks up tech debt, okay?

We've used a bunch of ways to avoid going into debt so far — keeping it to one feature at a time as much as possible, reviewing and committing as soon as something's done, even writing unit tests. But there's still some tech debt you just can't avoid. So in this post, we're going to talk about AI tech debt.

So, what is tech debt?

Some of you might not be sure what tech debt actually is, so let me spend a bit of time explaining it first.

Tech debt... in short, it's what you get from rushing.

What do I mean? Usually when we're building a project, we want to grab the market, hit a deadline, or just get the feature out first. So we might write code that isn't clean enough or consistent enough, skip proper testing, leave the docs incomplete, and so on. All of that is quality we temporarily sacrifice to ship fast.

And that sacrificed quality is what we call "tech debt."

Here's an everyday example. Say we buy a house and move everything in really fast, but all the cardboard boxes just get tossed in a corner. As long as you can start living there and using the place, who cares, right? But a while later, you find out that finding one charging cable means digging through three to five boxes, because when you moved in, you never really thought about where anything should go.

Code works the same way. The same code, the same logic in two places, so you keep changing file A and forgetting file B. Or the docs say one thing and the code does another. None of it breaks anything right now, but once you need to maintain or extend the project, you start paying interest. That's the idea behind tech debt.

So why bring this up? Because the Vibe Coding way of building actually makes it easy to pile up a ton of tech debt.

With traditional fast development, each round might only leave behind a little crap (as in bad code). But Vibe Coding doesn't just speed up development — it speeds up the crap too.

Take stock first, don't rush into refactoring

Cleaning up tech debt is what we call "refactoring." The definition of refactoring is "change the structure, not the behavior." In other words, the point of refactoring is to make the code cleaner, more consistent, and easier to maintain, without changing what the program does. That's also why I planned a whole testing day earlier in the series.

Refactoring can make your code cleaner, more consistent, and easier to maintain, sure — but at the end of the day you're still changing code. There's no guarantee the result after your changes matches what you had before, which is why tests are often called a "safety net."

So how do we get started? It really comes down to one thing: "taking inventory."

Open up our practice project again, go into Claude Code, and type /clear in the chat box to make sure the conversation is wiped. Then press Shift+Tab to switch to Plan Mode (you're good once you see plan mode on), and type:

Please take inventory of this project's tech debt:

- Duplicated logic
- Oversized components (more than 300 lines)
- Inconsistent patterns

Plus anywhere the code doesn't match CLAUDE.md or the existing docs.

This time I only want the list, no change plan. Give each item a severity and a recommendation.

Next you should see a list of suggested changes, and that's the tech debt list the AI pulled together for us.

But you'll notice I'm using Plan Mode for the inventory instead of just asking the AI to do it in Accept Edits Mode. Why?

Think of the AI as a really overeager helper. It's taking inventory... taking inventory... and then for whatever reason it just starts fixing things while it's at it. Next thing you know, there's a pile of Diffs (change records), and you don't have time to decide which changes should happen and which shouldn't. That's why I do the inventory in Plan Mode, so you can read the list first and then decide whether to change anything.

I bet you're thinking: "Can't I just write 'don't change anything yet' in the prompt?"

Honestly, that's not wrong. But if its Context blows up, it'll forget that eventually anyway, which is why I recommend doing the inventory in Plan Mode.

Pretty handy, right? This way we can quickly find the tech debt in the project and use the severity to decide whether to fix each item.

But before you start, you absolutely have to make sure your tests are all passing right now (all green). Otherwise you'll have no way to tell whether something was already broken or whether you just broke it!

The four kinds of debt AI racks up most

I want to pull one thing out here and look back at that prompt, because I specifically called out four things in it:

  • Duplicated logic: The same feature or task written two or more times.
  • Oversized components: One file crammed with too many jobs, more than N lines.
  • Inconsistent patterns: The same thing written different ways in different places.
  • Docs that don't match the code: CLAUDE.md, SPEC.md, and the code saying different things.

So why call out these four in particular? Because they're the debts AI racks up most often.

The root cause still comes back to the Context thing we keep talking about. Every time you use the AI, it's actually starting from zero. Unless you've written this stuff into specific files and use CLAUDE.md or SPEC.md to point the AI at them, it has no idea how your earlier code was written.

That's a lot of stuff. Pay it all back at once?

Honestly, no. But you can't ignore it either.

You should pick out the items with the biggest impact first, fix those, and keep updating step by step, instead of trying to do it all in one go.

Of course, there's one thing I still need to stress here:

The high, medium, and low the AI gives you are just its opinion, not gospel. You're the owner of this project, so you decide which debts to pay off first.

If you're not sure, think back to what we said about the MVP in earlier days: get the most important features right first and take your time with the rest. For an expense tracker, the core thing is that the "calculations" can never be wrong. Anything else can wait, as long as it doesn't get in the way of using the app.

And since that's a Plan Mode result, don't forget to have the AI save it. You can type:

Please save that tech debt list in full as docs/TODO.md, keeping the severity and recommendation for each item. Don't work on any of them yet.

After that, just take your time reading through TODO.md.

Let's try paying off some debt

Now let's actually pay off some tech debt. In my case, one of the items the AI found was that the formatting Hook we set up on Day 22 has no Prettier config file. So it's been formatting everything with Prettier's own defaults (double quotes, semicolons), while the project's existing code uses single quotes and no semicolons.

That means every time the AI changes a file from now on, that file gets formatted in a different style. That's exactly the inconsistent patterns we just talked about, and it counts as tech debt too. On top of that, the src/hook-test.js we used back then to test the Hook is still sitting in the project.

This one's relatively small, so there's no real need to open Plan Mode for it. Just ask the AI to do it in Accept Edits Mode.

Please add a Prettier config file, .prettierrc. Base the rules on the style of the project's existing code (quotes, semicolons, line width). Don't use Prettier's defaults.

Once it's added, run npx prettier --check src once to confirm that almost none of the existing files need to change. While you're at it, delete src/hook-test.js, which was left over from testing the Hook earlier.

When you're done, run npm test once, and mark the "No Prettier config file" item in docs/TODO.md as done.

.prettierrc is Prettier's config file. You can set your code formatting rules in it, like whether to use single or double quotes, whether to add semicolons, the max line length, and so on.

Notice I didn't tell it whether to use single or double quotes. I asked it to go look at the existing code style on its own.

Review: with refactoring, you're checking that nothing changed

Finally, say you're done refactoring. You absolutely need to have the AI run these:

  • npm test: Confirms the money-calculation logic wasn't touched. All those tests you spent time writing on Day 23 become your safety net today.
  • npm run build: Confirms the project still builds and runs, since a refactor can move a lot of files around.
  • Click through the screens yourself: You could use some automated testing tools to check the screens, but we're mainly reviewing whether the features are correct, so this layer is all on you.

Running them is easy too. Just give it this prompt:

Please run the following commands and report the results back to me:

1. npm test
2. npm run build

I'll leave the rest for you to try refactoring on your own.

How often should you take inventory?

I don't think there's really a standard answer here. You can decide how often based on the project's size, complexity, and how far along it is.

For example... with our expense tracker app, from the day we started until now, we never took inventory once. And today the first inventory turned up 30 items. That's not a huge number, but I'd still recommend dealing with it early.

So if I had to give you a rule, instead of counting by "how often," I'd suggest going by "timing." Take inventory whenever you hit one of these moments:

  • After a big redesign: Like when we reworked the screens in earlier days. That's a good time to tidy up while you're at it.
  • When the AI starts acting weird: Like fixing A breaks B, or it writes another copy of something that already exists.
  • Before launch: No matter what, I'd recommend checking at this point, since real users are going to be using it.

I also turned today's workflow into a diagram:

flowchart TD
    A["Confirm tests are all green<br>git status is clean"] --> B["Take inventory in Plan Mode<br>list only, no change plan"]
    B --> C["Save the list as docs/TODO.md"]
    C --> D{"Pay off the biggest-impact items first<br>How many files does it touch?"}
    D -->|"Add config, update docs"| F["Just ask the AI to do it"]
    D -->|"Touches several files"| G["Plan Mode<br>one item at a time"]
    F --> H{"Review<br>tests, build, screens all unchanged?"}
    G --> H
    H -->|"Pass"| I["Commit, one change per commit"]
    H -->|"Fail"| J["Roll back to the previous commit<br>shrink the scope and try again"]

Wrapping up

We're about at the end, so here's a quick recap:

  • Tech debt isn't a bug. It's something that doesn't hurt now but will hurt later. The AI only looks at one task at a time, so going back to clean up is something you have to kick off.
  • The four debts AI racks up most: duplicated logic, oversized components, inconsistent patterns, and docs that don't match the code.
  • Take inventory in Plan Mode, save the list in the project, and pay off the biggest-impact items first. Just do the small stuff directly; anything that needs real surgery goes through Plan Mode, one item at a time.
  • With refactoring, you're checking that nothing changed. Only commit once tests, build, and the screens all pass. If something fails, roll straight back instead of forcing a fix.

The debt's been inventoried and the tests are all green, so tomorrow we're deploying the app and giving it a real public URL.

Hope this post helped you pay off your debt. See you tomorrow!

entry.title: 30 Days of Vibe Coding | Day 23: Tests as Your Safety Net — Unit Testing with Vitest
entry.content:
Intro

"People can't be trusted."

Ever heard that one? From a security point of view, a lot of security holes come down to human error.

People forget, cut corners, and act on a whim. No matter how careful you are, something will still slip through.

So in this post we're going to look at a concept built on "people can't be trusted": testing.

So what is "testing"?

For a lot of beginners, testing is probably a pretty unfamiliar word.

But you've actually already been doing it. It's the "review" step I keep going on about.

Every time you asked the AI to change a feature or add a new one, I had you run through the review again and again to make sure nothing broke — things like adding an expense, checking whether it shows up in the list, refreshing to see if the data is still there, and so on.

So what we're going to do now is turn that "testing process" into something automated — a program that does all of this for us.

Not sure why that's a big deal? In short, review work that used to take you hours becomes something that runs on its own at the push of a button.

On top of that, it becomes what's called a "safety net." Whenever you change the code, this safety net checks whether anything got broken, so you don't end up changing feature A, breaking feature B, and never finding out.

Pick what to test

Huh? You have to be picky about what you test?

Yep. Not every feature needs tests. Picking the feature that would hurt "the most" if it broke and testing that is the most efficient way to go.

So which features count as the ones that hurt "the most"? For our money-note, it's anything to do with calculating money.

Which ones are those? For example...

  • sumAmount: Adds up every amount for the month (that's the total at the very top of the screen)
  • buildCategoryStats: How much each category spent and what share it takes. The stats page's pie chart and breakdown both use its results

I know you probably haven't seen these two pieces of code — I mean, who actually reads the code when they're Vibe Coding? (lol) But there were clues along the way. Back on Day 13, I said this:

One file is in charge of "calculating" (mine is src/utils/stats.js)

And I specifically pointed out...

Did the "calculating" part get pulled out into pure functions like we asked, instead of all being stuffed into the component?

All of that was set up and planned for this post. You could even call today the harvest.

So why use this as the thing we learn on? Simple: pure functions aren't tied to the UI or to storage, so they're the easiest to test. And when the logic is solid before it gets wired to the screen, it's easier to review too, because the result is either right or wrong — no gray area. Testing through the UI is a whole different story.

Getting started

Normally, the money-note project we've been working on doesn't have any testing packages or frameworks installed. So next we're going to ask the AI to add a testing framework for us and write the test cases. Before you start, don't forget to type /clear to wipe the conversation, so it doesn't read anything you two talked about earlier.

If all that sounds good, try this prompt to have it add a testing framework and write test cases:

Please add unit tests to this project. The focus is the money calculation logic — skip the UI for now.

Pay attention to these situations I especially care about:

- A month with no records at all
- When several categories have the same amount, the order can't jump around
- Percentages should just show whole numbers, not a long string of decimals

Please use Vitest as the testing framework, and add an npm test command. That command needs to exit on its own when it finishes, not sit there waiting.
After writing the tests, run them once. Then, if the existing docs (CLAUDE.md, SPEC.md) say anywhere that "no testing framework is installed," update those parts too.

Let's pause here for a second and look at what's special about this prompt.

First, I never mentioned the function names sumAmount or buildCategoryStats. Instead, I just described the situations I care about in plain language, and let the AI analyze things on its own, find those two functions, and write the test cases for me.

Not sure what situations to list? You can also look back at the SPEC.md we nailed down with the AI earlier. There's a section in it:

## 7. Acceptance criteria

Definition of done for v1:

1. Open it on a phone, the form is right on screen → enter 120 → tap "Food" → save, one expense recorded in three actions
2. The new entry shows up at the top of the list right away, and this month's total goes up to match
3. The pie chart slice sizes and the breakdown percentages correctly reflect that month's amount for each category
4. Tap any row in the list to edit the amount/category/date/note; after saving, the list and stats update to match
5. Deleting asks for confirmation first; once confirmed, that entry disappears from the list and the stats
6. Refresh the page, and all the data is still there
7. Switch to a month with no records, and it shows an empty state instead of a broken chart
8. Change an entry's date to last month, and it disappears from this month and shows up in last month
9. Press `◀` repeatedly to go back several months, then tap "This month" once to return to the current month; the "This month" button then disappears,
   and the left and right arrows in the month switcher don't shift position
10. **After adding an expense and switching to the stats page, total spending, the number of entries, and the pie chart all reflect the latest data**
11. Switching months on the stats page swaps the three numbers and the pie chart to that month; switching tabs doesn't reset the month back to this month

This is where you can think about it, or even ask the AI to use it as a reference for writing test cases, instead of letting the AI fill in the blanks on its own. That's exactly why I spent so much time earlier on how important SPEC.md is — it's the contract between you and the AI (of course, you can also flip through docs/plans to see the original plans).

Then it'll install Vitest, generate the test files, and tell you the results:

You can see my AI produced three test files with 57 test cases. It wrote way more than you'd probably expect.

If you go through the test files (*.test.js), you'll see stats.test.js, format.test.js, and useRecords.test.js all got tests. They cover the money calculations, formatting, and data filtering logic, respectively.

Adding .test to test file names is a convention. Some projects also put them in a src/__tests__ folder. Either way, it's just so developers can quickly tell a file is a test file — there's no special meaning beyond that.

If you try this yourself and end up with a different number of tests or different test cases, that's totally normal. AI has some randomness built in, so the number of cases won't be the same every time. We're just doing our best to constrain its behavior with SPEC.md and the prompt, so the cases it generates stay within the boundaries we asked for.

Reading the test cases

Even though the AI writes the test cases, you still need to roughly understand what they're testing and what they say. Otherwise, how would you know the tests it wrote are right?

The good news is that test cases are a lot easier to read than regular code, because most of them are just "put this in, expect that out." You only need to understand what's being tested.

Here's one I picked at random from my project (src/utils/format.test.js):

describe('formatAmount', () => {
  it('0 顯示成 $0', () => {
    expect(formatAmount(0)).toBe('$0')
  })

  it('三位數以內沒有逗號', () => {
    expect(formatAmount(999)).toBe('$999')
  })

  it('千分位逗號，前面加 $', () => {
    expect(formatAmount(1200)).toBe('$1,200')
    expect(formatAmount(12480)).toBe('$12,480')
    expect(formatAmount(1234567)).toBe('$1,234,567')
  })
})

This is testing the formatAmount function: give it different numbers, and see whether the output matches what we expect (toBe()).

Still confusing? No worries, I'll go through it line by line:

  • describe('formatAmount', ...): Groups the test cases inside it together. You usually put the name of the function being tested here, so you know what this group is testing.
  • it('0 顯示成 $0', ...): This is a single test case, with a description of the case inside. The description is usually the expected result (this one reads "0 shows as $0").
  • expect(formatAmount(0)).toBe('$0'): This is the core of the whole test. expect() means "I expect," and inside the parentheses goes the actual result. toBe() means "the result has to be exactly this." So the whole line in plain English is: I expect formatAmount(0) to come out as exactly $0.

So a test case is just a description of "put this in, expect that out." You've probably noticed tests are a lot easier to read than code, because they describe "how this function behaves." Whether that behavior matches what we expect is exactly what testing is for.

In software engineering, there's an approach called "Test-Driven Development (TDD)," where you write the test cases first, then write the code, and finally run the tests to see if they pass. This way you think through how the function should behave before you write any code, which helps you avoid writing code that doesn't do what you expected.

Controlled failure exercise: make it fail once

Next, we're going to make a mistake on purpose. Yep, you read that right — on purpose. Otherwise, how would you know the tests actually work? And having a failing case is what shows you what tests are really worth.

First, give the AI this prompt:

Please deliberately break formatAmount so the "thousands separator" case is missing the $ in front, then run the tests once and show me the results.

If all goes as expected, you should see the AI tell you the tests failed.

With tests as your safety net, whenever you add or change a feature, the tests will fail if you didn't update the test cases to match, or if you broke the existing code. Then you know what you broke, and it's a lot easier to track down the problem.

But once you've seen it fail, remember to change it back, or your project really will stay broken. The easiest way is to just tell the AI:

Please restore the formatAmount you just broke on purpose, then run the tests again to confirm everything passes.

And since we've brought up TDD anyway, here's a Mermaid diagram showing what a proper TDD workflow looks like:

flowchart TD
    A["List the scenarios this feature has"] --> B["Pick one and write it as a test"]
    B --> C["Run all the tests<br>the new one has to fail<br>this step is called red"]
    C --> D["Write just enough code to make it pass"]
    D --> E["Run them again, everything passes<br>this step is called green"]
    E --> F["Clean up the code with the tests protecting you<br>this step is called refactor"]
    F --> B

Try it: connect it to yesterday's Hook

No matter which step you're at or how far along the build is, there's one thing you'll keep doing over and over: npm test. But you don't have to remember it yourself or keep telling the AI — especially since the AI might forget about it once the Context gets too long.

So we can use a Hook to run the tests automatically. That way, every time the AI finishes something, it's guaranteed to run the tests for you, and you never have to worry about forgetting.

I'm not going to walk through how to do it here, though. Give it a try yourself!

Wrapping up

We're about at the end, so here's a quick summary:

  • Testing turns the manual review you've been doing all along into an automated program.
  • You don't need to test everything. Start with the part where a mistake would hurt the most.
  • You don't need to understand the code to direct the AI to write tests. Your prompt just needs to clearly describe the situations you care about.
  • Test cases are a lot easier to read than code — it's just "put this in, expect that out."

One last reminder, though: passing tests doesn't mean the feature has no problems. A lot of the UI/UX on screen still needs you to review it yourself.
