entry.title: 30 Days of Vibe Coding | Day 22: Hooks — Claude Code's Lifecycle Triggers
entry.content:
Intro

We're about to head into Week 4, which is also the final week of the whole series.

So what are we doing starting this week? I want to introduce the AI's "lifecycle triggers": Hooks.

The idea is that they hook into the AI's lifecycle and run specific commands at specific moments. None of this involves any AI judgment at all — it's pure system-level automation.

The idea behind Hooks: the lifecycle

AI actually has this concept called a "lifecycle." I know a lot of you might be thinking...

"Huh? Lifecycle? AI has a lifecycle too?"

In short, while the AI is working on a task, it goes through certain events, for example:

  • Before a tool runs (PreToolUse)
  • After a tool runs (PostToolUse)
  • Every time the AI finishes responding (Stop)
  • When it needs your attention (Notification)

These four are basically the lifecycle events you'll use the most. When one of them happens, we can attach our own Hook to it, so it automatically runs the command we want.

These Hook settings go in the project's config file, usually in the hooks block of settings.json.

So what's settings.json? We haven't really talked about it so far. It's the AI's config file — permissions, Hooks, and settings like that all live in there. And just like the Skills we covered on Day 15, it comes in two levels:

  • On your computer (~/.claude/settings.json): Shared across all of your own projects.
  • In the project (.claude/settings.json): Only used by this project, and it gets committed along with the project, so your teammates get the same settings when they pull it down.

There's also a .claude/settings.local.json. It lives in the project too, but it's just for you personally and doesn't get committed to Git. We'll use it for the second Hook in a bit.

At this point you might be wondering: how is this any different from just writing a rule in CLAUDE.md?

Roughly speaking, it's the difference between "please do this" and "you have to do this."

Not quite clicking? Earlier we covered CLAUDE.md, the rules and constitution for the AI to read. It gets loaded every time you start a new conversation. But even though we call it a constitution, a set of rules, there's still a good chance it gets forgotten, especially once the Context gets too long. So CLAUDE.md is more of a "please do this" thing — the AI does its best to follow it, but there's no guarantee it remembers every time.

A Hook, on the other hand, is an automated mechanism built at the system level. Whenever the AI performs a certain action or hits a certain event, the Hook fires, every single time, without going through the AI's judgment at all. So it's way more enforceable than CLAUDE.md.

So when do people usually use it? The simplest example is "format a file after it's been changed." Something that has to happen every single time is a great fit for a Hook, and there's no need for the AI to make a judgment call on it.

So next we're going to actually build two Hooks: a shared PostToolUse formatting Hook, and a personal Stop desktop notification Hook.

You've probably noticed I keep stressing how important Context is. No matter which plan you're on, or even if you're calling the API directly, the most expensive thing with AI is always tokens, and using your Context wisely.

Build #1: auto-format a file as soon as it's changed

Now let's see what Hooks can actually do, starting with the simplest one: formatting.

First, there's one thing you need to do: create a .claude/hooks folder in the money-note project. This folder is where the Hook scripts go.

Next, we'll install a new package in this project called Prettier. It's a code formatter that tidies up indentation, quotes, semicolons and so on according to a fixed set of rules, so all the code in your project looks consistent. Same as before, open your terminal, go to the project folder, and type:

npm install -D prettier

Of course, you can also be a little lazy and give the AI this prompt to install it for you:

Please install Prettier in the money-note project and add it to devDependencies.

If your project already has Prettier installed, just skip this step.

Before we paste in any code, here's how this Hook works:

  1. The AI uses the Edit or Write tool to change a file.
  2. The moment the change is done, the PostToolUse event fires, and the AI checks settings.json for any Hook attached to that event.
  3. If there is one, it runs the command in that Hook and hands it a JSON report of "what just happened." The JSON includes which tool was used this time and which file was changed.
  4. Our custom command then receives that JSON, pulls the file path out of it, and runs Prettier on that file.

I drew this out as a flowchart too:

flowchart TD
    A["AI changes a file<br>with Edit or Write"] --> B["PostToolUse event fires"]
    B --> C{"Is there a Hook attached<br>in settings.json?"}
    C -->|"No"| D["Do nothing"]
    C -->|"Yes"| E["Run the Hook's command<br>and hand it a JSON report"]
    E --> F["Script gets the file path from the JSON"]
    F --> G["Run Prettier on that file"]

So we need two things:

  • A script that receives the JSON and runs Prettier.
  • A setting that tells the AI "run this script on PostToolUse."

Next, create the file .claude/hooks/format-edited-file.mjs in the project and paste in the following (or, of course, just throw this at the AI and have it create the file for you):

import { spawnSync } from 'node:child_process'
import { isAbsolute, relative, resolve } from 'node:path'

let raw = ''
for await (const chunk of process.stdin) raw += chunk

try {
  const input = JSON.parse(raw)
  const filePath = input.tool_input?.file_path
  if (!filePath) process.exit(0)

  const projectRoot = resolve(process.env.CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR || process.cwd())
  const target = isAbsolute(filePath) ? resolve(filePath) : resolve(projectRoot, filePath)
  const pathFromRoot = relative(projectRoot, target)

  if (pathFromRoot.startsWith('..') || isAbsolute(pathFromRoot)) process.exit(0)

  const prettierBin = resolve(projectRoot, 'node_modules/prettier/bin/prettier.cjs')
  const result = spawnSync(process.execPath, [prettierBin, '--write', '--ignore-unknown', target], {
    cwd: projectRoot,
    stdio: ['ignore', 'inherit', 'inherit'],
  })

  process.exit(result.status ?? 0)
} catch (error) {
  console.error('格式化 Hook 無法讀取輸入：', error.message)
  process.exit(1)
}

You don't need to spend much time on the code above. It basically just does three things:

  • Takes in the JSON the AI hands over in step 3, then finds the file that was changed, which is tool_input.file_path.
  • Checks that the file really is inside the project folder.
  • Runs Prettier on that one file.

Next, we hook the script up in .claude/settings.json, so it runs automatically whenever the PostToolUse event happens:

{
  "hooks": {
    "PostToolUse": [
      {
        "matcher": "Edit|Write",
        "hooks": [
          {
            "type": "command",
            "command": "node \"${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR}/.claude/hooks/format-edited-file.mjs\""
          }
        ]
      }
    ]
  }
}

Pretty short, right? Don't worry, I'll go through it piece by piece:

  • PostToolUse: The lifecycle event, meaning it fires after a tool finishes running.
  • matcher: Sets a filter, so it only fires after the two file-editing tools, Edit and Write, finish. Reading files or running commands won't trigger it.
  • command: The command you want to run. Here we use Node to run the script from earlier. ${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR} is a variable Claude Code provides, and it points to the project's root directory.

Once you save, Claude Code should pick up the config change on its own, but to be safe you can restart it once to make sure it really loaded the settings.

So how do we test it? Easy — give the AI this prompt:

Please use the Write tool to create src/hook-test.js with any small function in it. Deliberately mess up the indentation and spacing, leave out the semicolons, and just write it straight in — no need to check or format it.

You should see it write something really messy:

But... when you actually open src/hook-test.js, you'll find the formatting has already been cleaned up nice and neat.

There's a reason I specifically wrote "use the Write tool" in the prompt. The Hook's matcher only looks at the Edit and Write tools. If the AI writes the file out with a Bash command instead (like cat > file), then... the Hook won't run. That's why I deliberately told it to use the Write tool.

Build #2: notify me when it's done

This next Hook is one I actually use myself. I pretty often hand the AI tasks that take a while to run, and I can't just sit there staring at the terminal the whole time, right?! I'm definitely going to use that time for small things that can be interrupted. So I wrote a Stop Hook that pops up a desktop notification every time the AI finishes responding.

Now, a quick heads-up about this example: it's macOS-only, so I don't recommend using it on Windows or Linux, since their desktop notification commands are different. Also, notifications like this are usually more of a "personal" thing, so I'd put it in .claude/settings.local.json, not the shared .claude/settings.json — otherwise your teammates will start getting notifications as soon as they pull the project lol.

So create .claude/settings.local.json and paste in the following:

{
  "hooks": {
    "Stop": [
      {
        "hooks": [
          {
            "type": "command",
            "command": "osascript -e 'display notification \"money-note 的任務完成了\" with title \"Claude Code\"'"
          }
        ]
      }
    ]
  }
}

osascript is a macOS-only command. Also, Stop doesn't have a matcher to set, so you can just write hooks directly here.

One more thing to watch out for: .gitignore usually doesn't exclude .claude/settings.local.json, since it's a file you create by hand. So add it to .gitignore yourself, so you don't accidentally commit it to Git.

Once you've added the Hook above, let's try triggering it. You can send the AI pretty much any prompt, for example:

Hello! How are you today?

If all goes well, you'll get a macOS desktop notification telling you "money-note 的任務完成了" ("the money-note task is done").

Easy, right? Hooks are really powerful — I've even hooked mine up to my Discord channel.

Hooks are a double-edged sword

Before we finish, there's one more thing I need to point out. Hooks are really powerful, and their value comes from being enforced — but that's also exactly where the risk is.

What do I mean? When a rule in CLAUDE.md has a problem or is written wrong, the AI can use its own judgment to fix it or work around it. But if your Hook has a bug, it'll blow up every single time it fires, and it won't make any judgment calls for you.

So what I'd recommend is: talk it through with the AI, have the AI write the Hook script for you, then test it in your own terminal first. Only after you've confirmed it works should you hook it up. That cuts out a lot of unnecessary trouble.

For example, you can test this script by handing it some JSON with no file path. If everything's fine, it'll exit quietly without any errors:

printf '%s' '{"tool_input":{}}' | node .claude/hooks/format-edited-file.mjs

Wrapping up

That pretty much covers this one, so let's do a quick summary again:

  • A Hook is a mechanism attached to the AI's lifecycle. It runs as soon as the event happens, without going through the AI's judgment. CLAUDE.md is "please do this," a Hook is "you have to do this."
  • Hook settings go in the hooks block of settings.json. Shared ones go in the project's .claude/settings.json and get committed with it. Personal ones (like desktop notifications) go in .claude/settings.local.json — remember to add that file to .gitignore yourself.
  • matcher decides which tools trigger the Hook. This time it only watches Edit and Write, so the AI writing a file with Bash won't trigger it.
  • Hooks are enforced, so if the command is broken, it blows up every time it fires. Test it in the terminal before hooking it up.

Tomorrow we'll talk about testing. Remember the code Day 14 said you could let slide for now because a mistake there wouldn't hurt much? It's time someone kept an eye on it for you.

I hope this post gave you a better feel for Hooks.

See you tomorrow on Day 23.

entry.title: 30 Days of Vibe Coding | Day 21: Week 3 Wrap-Up — Skills, Subagents, or MCP? How to Choose
entry.content:
Intro

Somehow we've already made it to the end of Week 3.

So this post pulls together the three ways we've covered for extending and powering up the AI — Skills, subagents, and MCP — so you're less confused about which one to reach for in practice.

What each one is for

Over the past week we met Skills, subagents, and MCP one at a time, and each of them has its own job:

  • Skill: Teaches the AI a method or workflow, so it does things the way you expect. Like the commit-message Skill we used earlier, where we taught the AI how to write commit messages, or bringing in the Frontend Design rules so the AI knows how the front-end UI should be designed.
  • Subagent: You spend money (tokens) to hire a specialist for a specific job. Like the code-reviewer subagent from earlier — we hired a specialist to review our code and report the results back to us.
  • MCP: A universal adapter that lets the AI talk to things outside your project. Like when we used Context7 MCP, we let the AI look up official docs directly. You can also hook it up to external tools like GitHub or Figma, so the AI can talk to them directly.

I also put all of this into a table so you can compare them:

SkillSubagentMCP
What it isA document that teaches the AI a method/workflowAn AI clone with its own separate ContextAn adapter that connects to external services
When it loadsOnly expands the full text when it's neededOnly opens a new room when you send it outTakes up a chunk of the desk as soon as it's connected, and only expands the full definitions when it's actually used
Context costLow — normally it only takes up a one-line descriptionLow for the main Agent, since all the work stays locked in the clone's own room (but the clone itself still spends tokens)Relatively high — tool names sit on the desk permanently, and whatever it fetches eats tokens too
Good forThe same approach used over and overWork you can hand off and just get the conclusion backTouching anything outside the project folder

There's one thing I really want to stress here: these three aren't mutually exclusive. They work together. Picking a Skill doesn't mean you can't use MCP, and picking a subagent doesn't mean you can't use a Skill. Don't forget the Context7 MCP example from earlier — it used a Skill and a Rule at the same time. MCP handled looking up the docs, while the Skill and the Rule told the AI when it should go look things up. That's a real example of stacking several of these together.

When to use which?

Now that you know what each one is for, the next step is figuring out how to choose.

Basically, you can use these three questions to decide what to use and when:

  1. Is this the same approach you'll reuse over and over? If yes, write a Skill. Anything you have to do every single time can become a Skill — like the commit message format, front-end UI design rules, the steps for looking up official docs, and so on.
  2. Is this work you could hand off and just get the conclusion back? If yes, create a subagent. Work that eats up a lot of Context — like code review, research, or scanning a big chunk of the project — is a great fit for a subagent. Let it finish the job and report the results back to you.
  3. Does it need to touch anything outside the project folder? If yes, hook up an MCP. Things like the browser, an internal database, Figma, GitHub, and so on all belong to the world outside your project folder, and that's when you need MCP.

Here's a flowchart too, so it's easier to see when each one fits:

flowchart TD
    A{"Same approach<br>reused over and over?"} -->|"Yes"| B["Write a Skill"]
    A -->|"No"| C{"Can it be handed off<br>for just the conclusion?"}
    C -->|"Yes"| D["Create a subagent"]
    C -->|"No"| E{"Is it the world outside<br>the project folder?"}
    E -->|"Yes"| F["Hook up an MCP"]
    E -->|"No"| G["Just add a rule to CLAUDE.md"]

So what if, as luck would have it, it's none of the three? Then just write a rule in CLAUDE.md. After all, CLAUDE.md is exactly the place for rules that can't be figured out just by reading the code.

Week 3 hands-on checklist

To wrap up Week 3, here's a checklist for you to go through once:

  • You know a Skill is just a folder plus a SKILL.md file, and you know the ones you write yourself go in .claude/skills/, while installed ones end up in ~/.claude/plugins/.
  • You installed Frontend Design with /plugin and used it to give the UI a full makeover.
  • After the UI changes, you ran through one round of testing (add, delete, refresh, check the stats) to make sure nothing got broken.
  • Your project has a DESIGN.md that passes lint validation, and it's hooked into CLAUDE.md with @DESIGN.md.
  • You tried both the automatic trigger of the commit-message Skill and the manual /commit-message trigger, and it lists the scope first and waits for your confirmation before committing.
  • You tried the code-reviewer subagent, sent it a job once by calling it by name or with @, and personally read the review results you got back.
  • You hooked up Context7 MCP, can see it's connected in /mcp, asked it a package question once, and watched it go look up the docs on its own.

Wrapping up

That's about it for Week 3.

You'll notice there's actually quite a lot of basic AI Agent knowledge to wrap your head around, and this is still just a drop in the ocean — I haven't even covered settings like Hooks and Rules yet. But I think what we've covered so far handles about 80% of use cases. The remaining 20% you can pick up gradually through real-world work, or go looking for when you need it.

If that all makes sense, let's move on to the next one.

entry.title: 30 Days of Vibe Coding | Day 20: MCP Basics — Make the AI Check the Latest Docs Before Answering
entry.content:
Intro

Remember how I said earlier that package versions are the thing AI's memory goes stale on most easily, and that's why you should still take a quick look at the versions in package.json yourself after installing?

We all know AI is built on huge amounts of training data, so it's easy for it to hand you outdated config, outdated package versions, or even outdated ways of writing code.

So in this post, we're going to look at something called MCP (Model Context Protocol).

What is MCP?

So what exactly is MCP? If you've been using AI since the early days, you've probably already run into this thing with the full name Model Context Protocol. If you got into AI more recently, you might actually be more familiar with Skills.

But the two aren't old and new versions of the same thing. Some people think Skills came along to replace MCP, but in reality, no matter how popular Skills get, they can't replace MCP. Plenty of services rely on MCP to talk to AI, and Context7, which we're demoing today, is one of them.

MCP is an open standard protocol proposed by Anthropic (the company that makes Claude). Not that easy to picture, right?

Put simply, think of it as a USB adapter for your computer (though personally I prefer using a hub as the example). It lets AI talk to outside services in one consistent way.

What does that mean? AI comes with some built-in limits, for example...

  • There isn't much it can do out of the box:
    • Read files
    • Edit files
    • Run commands
    • Search the web, and most of what it does stays inside your project folder.
  • Its training data has a cutoff date, so it won't know about anything that came out after that, like new package versions, new ways of doing things, or official docs that got rewritten.
  • And it definitely has no idea what data lives in your company's internal systems.

MCP was created to solve exactly these limits. As long as everyone follows this open standard protocol, AI can talk to all kinds of different tools in the same way. That's why you'll see a diagram like this one:

MCP is like an external hub for your computer: every time you plug something in, it gains another ability.

At this point your head might be spinning a little. We learned Skills, then Subagents, and now there's MCP too. Kind of a lot, right?

So let me take this chance to sort out the differences between Skills, Subagents, and MCP again. You can think of it like this:

  • Skill: Teaches the AI how to do things or follow a process, like how to write commit messages or how to use certain knowledge. These lean toward "knowledge and methods."
  • Subagent: Brings in a separate, clean little AI clone to do work for you. Like code-reviewer, which locks itself in its own little room, finishes reviewing the project, and only tosses the results back.
  • MCP: Lets your AI talk to outside services. Context7, which we're connecting today, lets it look up the latest official docs on its own. There are also ready-made MCPs for things like browsers and databases, so it can reach stuff beyond your project folder and its own training data.

I keep mentioning Context7, so what is it? It's pretty straightforward: it organizes the official docs for packages, so AI can look up the latest official docs instead of relying on what it remembers from training.

You might be thinking: can't Claude Code already search the web on its own?

Yes, it can. But what a regular web search pulls back isn't always for the right version, and it's often mixed in with outdated tutorials. Context7 specifically organizes each package's official docs, matches them to versions, and includes sources. That's the difference.

Here's how it relates to the AI:

Now let's actually try it out.

Connecting Context7 MCP

Most MCPs are pretty easy to install. Usually it's just a single command.

Context7, for example, provides an install command. Open your terminal and type:

npx ctx7 setup

If you don't have Node installed, this command won't work, so make sure you install Node.js first.

In the terminal, just pick the AI you use, like below (I'm using Claude Code here):

Context7 now also offers a CLI + Skill option, but here I'm still demoing the MCP Server route.

Next you should get a URL:

That URL is Context7's authorization link. Copy it into your browser, and you'll be asked to log in and authorize it.

Once authorization succeeds, your terminal should show a screen like this, which means Context7 MCP is installed!

Now let's check the MCP status. Type /mcp inside Claude Code, and you'll see that context7 is connected.

Next, let's try to get Context7 called. Open the project we've been practicing on (money-note) and start Claude Code. Once you're in, ask a question about package versions. Type this:

Please check which version of Tailwind this project uses, look up the official docs, and tell me the biggest difference in configuration between v4 and v3.
Also check whether the way src/style.css is written right now is correct for v4.
Include the doc sources in your answer.

You should then see the AI go call Context7 MCP:

By the way, the context7 - query-docs (MCP) in the second screenshot is what an MCP tool looks like inside the AI. The first part is the server name, the middle is the tool name, and the MCP tag at the end reminds you that this is an external tool, not one built into the AI.

Pretty easy, right? You should then see the AI answer, with the doc sources included.

So why does it go look things up on its own?

At this point you might be wondering how the AI knew to use Context7 MCP. We never mentioned it in the question, after all.

That's because when we installed the MCP with npx ctx7 setup, Context7 didn't just install the MCP server. It also put a Skill on your computer, and that Skill tells Claude to check Context7 MCP first whenever it runs into a package question.

Don't believe me? Here's the description from that Skill:

---
name: context7-mcp
description: This skill should be used when the user asks about libraries, frameworks, API references, or needs code examples. Activates for setup questions, code generation involving libraries, or mentions of specific frameworks like React, Vue, Next.js, Prisma, Supabase, etc.
---

The description is basically saying "if the user asks about libraries, frameworks, or API references, or needs code examples, activate this Skill," and the Skill's content tells Claude how to go query Context7 MCP.

And it's not just the Skill. There's also a Rule telling Claude to check Context7 MCP for package questions. The Rule says pretty much the same thing: "whenever you're asked how to use or configure a library, framework, or SDK, look up the latest docs with Context7 first and then answer, even if you think you already know." Here's where these live:

  • Rule: ~/.claude/rules/context7.md. We haven't talked about this folder yet. The .md files in it are the same kind of thing as CLAUDE.md: Claude Code reads them in when it starts, and they apply to every project.
  • Skill: ~/.claude/skills/context7-mcp/SKILL.md. This one has the steps for looking up docs: first use resolve-library-id to find the right package, then use query-docs to pull the matching section.

And if it doesn't use context7? Also easy: just tell it to use context7 by name.

The reason Context7 MCP also installs a Skill and a Rule is to make Claude more proactive: when it hits a package question, it goes and looks it up on its own instead of waiting for you to call it out.

MCP isn't free

One last thing I want to point out: using MCP comes at a cost.

What cost? Even though MCP is a standard adapter, there's a backend application behind it. A remote server like Context7 runs on a remote machine, which is why it needs you to log in and authorize.

Sure, you can also run an MCP on your own computer so you don't have to log in. But then you're the one maintaining the MCP server's code, updates, server environment, and so on. For regular users, I think that's a lot more hassle.

MCP also takes up a lot of Context. Take the example above: every time Context7 MCP pulls docs, all that content gets dumped into the conversation in one go. That can easily eat a big chunk of Context, and then your AI starts forgetting earlier parts of the conversation. That's why MCP isn't free. It comes at a cost.

And it's not just the content it pulls back. Just connecting it takes up some desk space up front. Remember /context from Day 6? Try typing it:

You'll see a new MCP tools line. That's because once you connect an MCP, the names of its tools get put on the desk first, so Claude knows which tools it has. The full definition of each tool only gets opened up when it's actually used.

So my own habit is: connect it when you need it, and turn it off when you don't.

If you want to remove Context7 entirely, run this command. It removes the MCP, the Skill, and the rest together:

npx ctx7 remove --mcp --claude

If you're curious about other MCPs, check out modelcontextprotocol.io. There are tons of MCP servers you can use (like Figma, GitHub, and more).

Wrapping up

That's about it. Hopefully you've got the basic idea of MCP now, so here's a final rundown:

  • MCP is like an adapter that lets AI connect to outside tools or services in one consistent way.
  • Type /mcp to see which MCP servers are connected right now and how many tools each one brings.
  • Once an MCP server is connected, the AI decides on its own whether to use it based on the tool descriptions. Context7 also installs a Rule and a Skill to make it more proactive. If it really doesn't use it, call it out by name.
  • Connected MCPs take up desk space, so turn them on when you need them, and turn them off or remove them when you don't, to cut down on Context usage.

That's it for this one. See you in the next post.

entry.title: 30 Days of Vibe Coding | Day 19: Subagents — Hiring a Code Review Sidekick
entry.content:
Intro

We've learned quite a bit so far, especially about Skills. But... have you ever stopped to think about this?

"If we keep stuffing everything into the current AI, is the Context really going to be enough?"

Real-world projects are huge, after all. Isn't it way too easy for the Context to blow up?

That's why today we're looking at Subagents, which is basically a way to bring in "someone else." You can hand some of the work off to a separate AI clone, so your main conversation doesn't get stuffed full.

Why do you need Subagents?

First we need to get one idea straight: the difference between the "main agent" and a "subagent."

The "main agent" is the AI chat window you normally talk to. A "subagent" is a separate AI clone you bring in, but it isn't in the same chat window as you. It has its own separate context and its own world, and it only brings back what it finished (the conclusion).

So here's a question to think about:

If the AI in the main conversation can read the code itself, why bother handing Code Review (checking and reviewing the code) off to someone else?

The reason is simple, and it has a lot to do with Context.

What do I mean?

From earlier chapters, we know that if you stuff too much into Context, or worse, trigger Auto compact (the automatic compaction from Day 6), the AI loses the key points. So keeping an eye on how much goes into Context really matters. But in real development, we often work across a ton of files, sometimes even across projects. That's when Context gets huge, maybe even past the AI's memory limit, and naturally it gets bloated and its judgment suffers. This is what's called "Context Confusion": so much irrelevant information is crammed in that it actually leads the AI to make bad calls.

In plainer terms, "Context Confusion" is like uploading N files for it to reference when only 1 of them is actually needed. All the others are just noise, and that's what leads the AI to make bad calls.

Subagents are designed to solve exactly this problem. They give you these advantages:

  • A clean main agent: The AI in the main conversation doesn't get thrown off by earlier conversations or info from other files, so it can focus on the current task. The subagent only focuses on the task you gave it, and when it's done, it sends just the conclusion back to the AI in the main conversation.
  • Saving Context in the current conversation: Since the subagent has its own separate context, the AI in the main conversation doesn't need to read every file itself. That saves a lot of Context and lets the main AI stay focused on the current task.

The whole flow looks like this:

sequenceDiagram
    participant U as You
    participant M as Main agent (your chat window)
    participant S as Subagent (separate context)
    U->>M: Code review the whole project for me
    M->>S: Hand the Code Review off to the subagent
    Note over S: In its own world<br>opens files, reads code, digs around<br>none of it takes up the main conversation's context
    S->>M: Sends back only the review results
    M->>U: Sums up the results for you

So what does this have to do with Skills? A lot, actually.

But first, let's clear up a common misunderstanding:

A subagent is a brand-new, separate context, and it may not have access to the Skills we wrote yesterday. So if you assume a subagent automatically picks up your Skills and uses them, the answer is: not necessarily.

Why "not necessarily"? Because it's your call. Subagents can call the Skills in your project, sure. But the reviewer we're about to build will be restricted to reading files and searching, without even the ability to call Skills, so it really can't touch yesterday's Skill.

So... if it can't use Skills, how does it know "how to do the job"? That depends entirely on its definition file. We'll go through creating one in a bit, and it's really simple: it's just a markdown file, and that file is its job manual (SOP). You need to spell out its role, steps, and report format clearly. Same as a Skill, really.

Going by all that, does it mean Skills and subagents have nothing to do with each other and can't work together? Not quite. A subagent definition actually has a skills field that can preload existing Skills into the subagent, so it can use the Skills you already wrote to do its job.

So you can think of it like this:

  • Skill: teaches a method, so the AI learns how to do things by your rules.
  • Subagent: brings in a specialist who does the work for you without taking up the main conversation's context.
  • Agent: the AI in the main conversation, which hands tasks to subagents and sums up what comes back for you.

Once that clicks, we'll go build a Code Review subagent for real.

Building a code-reviewer subagent

So how do you create a subagent? It's a lot like yesterday's Skill, except it lives in .claude/agents/. And it's even simpler: you don't need a separate folder for each one like with Skills, because one subagent maps directly to one markdown file.

Again using our money-note project as the example, create a .claude/agents/ folder in the project root, add a code-reviewer.md inside it, and paste in this first version:

---
name: code-reviewer
description: Reviews code quality. Use when the user asks for a code review, a review, or to check the code. Read-only, no edits.
tools: Read, Grep, Glob
---

You are the senior frontend reviewer for the money-note project. When you get a review task:

1. First read SPEC.md, CLAUDE.md, and DESIGN.md to learn the project's rules
2. Review the code in the given scope, focusing on:
   - Bug risks: edge cases, gaps in data validation, state getting out of sync
   - Duplicate logic: the same thing written two or more times
   - Breaking project rules: amounts not converted to number, hardcoded colors instead of variables
   - Naming and readability
3. You can only read. Do not change any files

Report format: one item per issue, including
- Severity: Red (must fix) / Yellow (suggestion)
- Location: file and line number
- Problem and suggested fix (one sentence)

If there are no problems, say so plainly. Don't invent issues to fill space.

Recognize that frontmatter? Besides name and description, though, this time there's an extra tools field, which limits which tools this subagent can use.

The value of tools is Read, Grep, Glob, which means this subagent can only:

  • Read files
  • Search files
  • Not edit files or run commands

That's on purpose, because we want this subagent to only review code, not change it.

Read reads file contents Grep searches file contents Glob searches file paths

Same goes for the body: you need to spell out its role, task steps, and report format so it knows how to do its job.

Putting the subagent to work

Don't forget: after creating the subagent, restart Claude Code so it gets loaded. Otherwise the AI in the main conversation won't be able to find it. Quick clarification: you only need to restart the "first time you create the .claude/agents/ folder." After that, adding or editing files in it works just like Skills: save it and it takes effect.

Let's give it a quick spin, again using the money-note project. Type this into the Claude Code chat:

Please code review these files:

- src/App.vue
- src/components/
- src/assets/main.css

Please check whether they follow DESIGN.md, possible layout breaks at 375px, form labels, keyboard focus, and whether buttons are at least 44px.

src/assets/main.css is a file that doesn't exist. I typed it on purpose.

Then you'll probably run into a problem: the main agent just starts doing the work itself?!

Wait, why is the main agent doing the Code Review on its own?! Why isn't it calling the subagent? Is it broken?

Nope. The main agent decided it could handle this itself, so it just went ahead. In that situation, no matter how nicely you write the description, it won't help, because it thinks it can do the job (stubborn).

So what do we do? Simple: call out code-reviewer by name, like this:

Please use code-reviewer to check these files:

- src/App.vue
- src/components/
- src/assets/main.css

Please check whether they follow DESIGN.md, possible layout breaks at 375px, form labels, keyboard focus, and whether buttons are at least 44px.

Next you'll see a code-reviewer block show up at the bottom of the chat window. That means the main agent has handed the task to the subagent.

Oh, and remember the src/assets/main.css I deliberately got wrong? You can see the main agent looked through the folders before handing off the work, found that the file doesn't exist, checked CLAUDE.md on its own to figure out that the project's real stylesheet is src/style.css, and swapped that one in for review, all without stopping to ask me.

If you don't even want to gamble on whether the main agent will just do it itself, there's an even safer trick: type @ in the input box and a menu pops up where you can pick code-reviewer (agent). Pick that, and it's guaranteed to go to the subagent.

After a while, you'll see the review results the subagent reports back:

So does the name code-reviewer come from the filename (.md) or from the frontmatter name? The AI actually goes by the frontmatter name. So you could rename the file to code-reviewer-1.md, and as long as the frontmatter name is still code-reviewer, it'll still recognize it.

So once you've got this Code Review report, what do you do with it? Pretty much the same as Day 12: go through the report yourself and understand what it's saying. Anything you don't get, figure it out. That's the whole trick.

Wrapping up

That's about it, so here's a quick rundown of today's key points:

  • Subagent = a clone with its own separate context:
    • Lives in its own world
    • Only brings back the conclusion
    • Avoids Context pollution
  • Subagent definition files go in .claude/agents/. They're written a lot like Skills: the description says when to trigger it, and tools controls permissions.
  • Be clear when you hand work off. Using the @ menu guarantees it gets handed off.

See you in the next one.

entry.title: 30 Days of Vibe Coding | Day 18: Your First Skill — Writing SKILL.md from Scratch
entry.content:
Intro

So far we've been using stuff other people built (the official ones). But can the official stuff really cover everything we need? Honestly, that's pretty unlikely.

In this post we're going to build our own Skill, one made around what we personally need, so our workflow runs a little smoother.

A quick refresher on Skill structure

We did a quick intro to Skills earlier and looked at how they're structured:

.claude/
└── skills/
    └── commit-message/   ← this folder's name is the Skill's name
        └── SKILL.md

So at its core, a Skill is just a folder plus a Markdown file. The folder name is the Skill's name, and the Markdown file is the Skill's content.

You can create a Skill yourself, or ask the AI to create it for you. But knowing how to write one is a whole different thing, so I'm going to break down the structure of SKILL.md in detail, so you can build your own Skill.

Heads up: different AI vendors may put Skills in different places. Claude Code uses .claude/skills/ in your project, but Codex uses .agents/skills/, so put your Skills wherever your AI tool expects them.

Building a commit-message Skill

Right now our money-note project doesn't have a single Skill, so we're going to build one from scratch.

So... what Skill should we build? How about one that "automatically triggers" to write commit messages?

How do we write it? Basically, there are two ways a Skill gets called:

  • Automatic triggering.
  • Manual triggering.

Let's skip manual triggering for now and start with automatic triggering. Automatic triggering depends on the description inside the SKILL.md frontmatter, so how you write that description matters a lot.

frontmatter is the block at the very top of a SKILL wrapped in two --- lines. Think of it like the personal details at the top of a resume: that part is just for "information about this file." Blog posts often use it for the title, author, and date (the metadata for this very post lives in frontmatter too).

So how do you actually write a description? I think a good description covers three things:

  • When to trigger: when this Skill should kick in.
  • What it does: what this Skill actually does.
  • Important boundaries: the key limits of this Skill.

A bit hard to picture, right? So let's actually build a commit-message Skill and take it apart.

First, in your project root (using our money-note project as the example), create a .claude/skills/commit-message/ folder, add a SKILL.md inside it, and paste in this first version:

---
name: commit-message
description: Use when the user asks to commit, submit, or save changes. Check the scope of the changes first, propose an English commit message in this project's format, and only commit after the user confirms.
---

# Commit message rules

Format: `<type>: <one sentence describing what was done>`

## Types

- feat: new feature
- fix: bug fix
- style: visual tweaks (no logic changes)
- docs: documentation (SPEC, DESIGN, CLAUDE.md, etc.)
- refactor: refactoring (same behavior)
- test: tests
- chore: chores (config, packages, etc.)

## Rules

- Read git status and the diff first, and list the files you plan to commit; don't automatically add every untracked file
- If you see `.env`, keys, credentials, or a file you can't figure out, stop and flag it
- Propose the commit message and scope first, and only run git add and git commit after the user confirms
- Write the description in English and say "what was done," not "which file changed"
- For fix, the description should include the cause, so it's easier to dig through history later
- One commit per thing; if things got mixed together, split them first

## Examples

- feat: add a spending stats page with a pie chart
- fix: delete by id to avoid index mismatch after sorting

At this point, your project structure should look something like this:

Of course, you can also just hand all of this to the AI and let it create the file for you, so you don't have to do it by hand:

Please create `.claude/skills/commit-message/SKILL.md` in the project root with the following content:
---
name: commit-message
description: Use when the user asks to commit, submit, or save changes.

...(rest omitted)

The example Skill I'm giving you here is the most basic version of a commit-message Skill. Whenever the user asks to commit, submit, or save changes, the AI calls this Skill and follows its rules: check the scope of the changes first, propose a commit message in this project's format, and only commit after the user confirms.

So the description works kind of like search keywords on Google. Claude matches what the user is asking for against the description, and if it fits, the Skill triggers automatically. That's what "automatic triggering" means.

And "manual triggering"? That one's really simple. It's based on your folder name. Our folder is called commit-message, so the manual command is /commit-message, and that calls the Skill directly.

Some of you might be wondering: why not just load the whole Skill from the start, instead of matching the user's request against the description? The reason is simple:

It keeps the context from getting flooded

The AI doesn't normally spread every skill's full text out on the desk (that would eat way too much context). It only sees the names and descriptions, uses those to decide "does the current task need this one?", and only opens up the full content when there's a match.

There's also a recommended way to lay out the content of a Skill:

  1. Format: a skeleton you can understand at a glance, so you know how this Skill is structured.
  2. Rules: the basis for making judgment calls, so you know this Skill's rules.
  3. Examples: templates to imitate, so you know what this Skill's output looks like.

Notice anything? I'm teaching the AI the way I'd teach a person. This three-part structure is exactly the same as the "SOP for teaching people" we talked about earlier. For AI, examples work especially well. Following a template is way more reliable for it than reasoning from rules, so never skip the examples when you write a skill.

As for me, the Skills I actually use also have this info:

metadata:
  author: Ray
  version: "2026/09/01"

This metadata isn't required. A Skill only strictly requires name and description. metadata is an official field, not something I made up, but the AI doesn't do anything with it, so I just use it to hold the author and version.

So when should you turn something into a Skill? My rule of thumb: if you've said the same thing three or more times, write it up as a Skill, so you don't have to keep repeating yourself.

Of course, there are lots of other settings you can tweak in a Skill, like allowed-tools to limit which tools the Skill can use, disable-model-invocation to stop the AI from triggering it automatically so only you can call it manually, and you can even have a Skill take arguments like a slash command. We won't get into those today. You'll naturally run into them as you write more Skills, and the official docs have everything when you need it.

Wrapping up

That's about it for this post, so let's wrap things up:

  • You can create Skills for a project or for your personal preferences. Project Skills go in .claude/skills/, personal ones go in ~/.claude/skills/
  • description is the heart of automatic triggering, and writing it is simple: the more it reads like "Use when the user asks for X," the more easily it gets triggered automatically
  • The core content of a Skill has three parts:
    1. Format.
    2. Rules.
    3. Examples, and whatever you do, don't skip the examples.
  • When should you turn something into a Skill? Once you've said the same thing three or more times

See you tomorrow.

entry.title: 30 Days of Vibe Coding | Day 17: Making the UI Look Good (Part 2) — Locking In the Style with DESIGN.md
entry.content:
Intro

"Wait... why does the screen the AI changed this time look different from my original style?"

It's not just you. This happens all the time.

All the design style decisions we talked through (color palette, spacing, button hierarchy, copy tone) only exist in that one conversation's context. As soon as you close it or /clear to start a new chat, all of it disappears. Unless you specifically tell the AI to write those design decisions down in a document and lock them in, it'll keep improvising and guessing all over again.

So to solve that, in this post we're going to look at something called a design document (DESIGN.md).

Standing on the shoulders of giants: DESIGN.md

So why do we need this post and a design document at all? The main reason is that the AI's UI style is different every time, because design decisions usually only live in the current conversation's context. Once the conversation ends, they're gone.

Then whenever you ask the AI to build a new feature or component, it'll try to analyze and track down your previous design decisions and guess from reading the code, but it's hard for it to get right. That leads to all kinds of visual imbalance (inconsistent button colors, inconsistent spacing, inconsistent font sizes...). That's why we need a design document to lock in the style.

So here's the question: how do we actually fix this? Good news: Google has put together a standard format for design documents for us, called DESIGN.md.

It actually comes from Stitch, an AI design tool that can produce a UI from a one-sentence description. DESIGN.md is the design system format that grew out of Stitch, and in 2026 Google Labs open-sourced it on GitHub. The goal is to let every AI tool (Claude Code, Cursor, Copilot...) understand your design system using the same format.

You might notice that the official project and npm package use lowercase design.md (you'll see it in the commands coming up). To keep things consistent and easy to read, I'll just call it DESIGN.md in uppercase throughout this post.

So how does DESIGN.md solve the problem? Let me give you a scenario. Say you ask the AI to make a blue button. The AI might do this...

  • First time: #3B82F6
  • Second time: #2563EB
  • Third time: bg-blue-500

They're all blue, but... they're still slightly different. Those subtle differences make the screen feel unbalanced or even a bit weird, not to mention the problems once it's in a real product.

"Can't I just write these rules in CLAUDE.md? Isn't CLAUDE.md the supreme constitution?"

I bet that's the first thing that popped into your head. It's definitely one way to do it, but the DESIGN.md approach is better, because it splits design decisions into two layers:

  • YAML front matter: holds the exact design tokens (color codes, fonts, spacing, corner radius, components). This part is for machines to read precisely.
  • Markdown body: holds the design reasoning: why this color, when to use it, when it's off-limits. This part is for people (and the AI) to read.

That way, the AI doesn't just know "the primary color is #245C4A." It also knows "where this green is allowed to be used," and even what the overall design philosophy is. That cuts way down on the chances of it using the wrong color.

Let it hand in its own design doc

So how do we actually write this DESIGN.md? I'm sure a lot of people are wondering. And the answer is: have the AI put it together and write the DESIGN.md itself!

Remember the last line of yesterday's prompt, "When you're done, tell me which design decisions you made and why"? That line was actually laying the groundwork for today. The AI is the one that made the most design decisions during the whole makeover, so it knows them best. It's the perfect one to write this document.

It's simple. Just type the following prompt (manual mode on or accept edits on is all you need here, no need for Plan Mode):

Please run `npx @google/design.md spec` to learn the format DESIGN.md requires, then put this project's current design decisions together into a spec-compliant DESIGN.md in the root directory. The content must be based on the actual code (check the color codes against the tokens in src/style.css).

In the Markdown body, besides the officially recommended sections, please add an extra section called "Responsive and accessibility review" that includes review criteria like 375px / 768px and buttons being at least 44px tall.

If CLAUDE.md already has any styling-related rules, move them into DESIGN.md as well. Don't keep a copy in both places.

From now on, any UI-related change must follow the DESIGN.md spec, with no more changing things from memory. So please add this line at the top of CLAUDE.md:
See @SPEC.md for the spec and @DESIGN.md for the design guidelines. All UI-related changes must follow the design guidelines.

I bet you're full of question marks right now. Don't worry, let me explain three parts of it:

  • The npx @google/design.md spec in the first paragraph: This command outputs the format spec for "what a standard DESIGN.md should look like." So you're basically asking the AI to read the DESIGN.md spec first before starting. That way the file it writes actually follows the standard, instead of being something it made up.
  • "Move them into DESIGN.md as well" in the third paragraph: This is to avoid having one rule in two places. If you don't do this, there's a good chance you'll hit "changed A, forgot to change B," and you end up with documents fighting each other. So take the chance to clean it up now, and let the design guidelines live in just one place: DESIGN.md.
  • The @SPEC.md / @DESIGN.md in the last paragraph: The core point of this line is to make the AI automatically read the design guidelines (DESIGN.md) every time it starts a new conversation. As for the @... I'll explain that a bit later.

Here's a short excerpt of the DESIGN.md for reference. For the full file, check out the DESIGN.md in the project:

---
version: alpha
name: Money Note Warm Paper Ledger
description: Design system for a single-user expense tracker. Ink on paper, ledger column lines, a double underline under totals, numbers first, not a blue-and-white admin dashboard.
colors:
  # === Base colors ===
  paper: "#F3EFE7"
  card: "#FFFDF8"
  # === Ink colors ===
  ink: "#1F2925"
  ink-soft: "#56625C"

... (a bunch skipped)

# Money Note Design Guidelines

See [SPEC.md](./SPEC.md) for the implementation spec. This document only covers what the screens look like: color palette, type scale, spacing, component states, and review criteria.

**The single source of truth is the tokens in the code.** The values in the YAML front matter map one-to-one to the `@theme` block in `src/style.css` and to `src/constants/categories.js`. Change one side, and you have to change the other.

## Overview

Money Note is a personal expense tracker. The core scenario is "right after spending money, standing outside a convenience store, logging it on your phone." So the whole visual design serves just one thing: **letting the numbers be read the fastest and entered the fastest.**

The visual direction is a **warm-toned paper ledger**, not an admin interface. The screens should read like an open handwritten ledger: cream paper, dark ink, a horizontal ruled line for each entry, a vertical line in the amount column separating money from text, and the accounting-style double underline under the monthly total.

The three kinds of ledger lines carry information on their own (one row per entry, money and text in separate columns, a single line for subtotals and a double line for totals), so using them as the layout skeleton means no extra decoration is needed. **Hierarchy always comes from line weight and the two layers of paper/card background, not from shadows, rounded corners, or the number of colors.**

The mood should be quiet, trustworthy, and easy on the eyes, closer to a "tool" than an "app." No gradients, glass effects, emoji icons, over-the-top shadows, or walls of colorful tags. The most eye-catching thing on the screen is always the monthly total, and everything else steps back behind it.

Pretty handy, right? Just have the AI put it together, and you don't have to figure out the YAML format or how to write the Markdown sections yourself.

Design docs have a linter too

What do I mean by "design docs have a linter too"? In short, a linter is a tool that "checks" a specific format. ESLint, Stylelint, and Markdownlint are all examples. And DESIGN.md? Of course it has its own linter too.

So why bring this up? Because unless you're familiar with DESIGN.md, it's really hard to spot by eye whether the AI got the format right. Luckily, the official project provides a linter to help with that, so you can type the following prompt and have the AI check whether your DESIGN.md has any problems:

Please run `npx @google/design.md lint DESIGN.md` to check whether DESIGN.md follows the DESIGN.md spec, and report the results back to me.

So what does lint actually check? Mainly these:

  • Whether the YAML structure is correct, whether colors includes the required primary, and whether any recommended sections are missing
  • Whether any token references are broken (like {colors.primery} missing an "a," or using a property the spec doesn't recognize)
  • Whether there are orphan tokens that are "defined but never used"
  • Whether it passes WCAG AA contrast

Super handy, right?

If you're on Windows and DESIGN.md doesn't seem to respond, .md might be getting swallowed by the file association. Try npx -p @google/design.md designmd lint DESIGN.md instead.

Adding it to the constitution

Don't think we're done just because we covered all that. Even with a DESIGN.md design document keeping things in check, you have to make sure the AI automatically reads it every time a new conversation starts. Otherwise it'll still forget.

So we need to add this line to CLAUDE.md:

See @SPEC.md for the spec and @DESIGN.md for the design guidelines. Any UI-related change must follow the DESIGN.md guidelines.

Of course, you can also just hand this line to the AI and have it add it for you, so you don't have to edit the file by hand.

Please add this line at the top of CLAUDE.md:
See @SPEC.md for the spec and @DESIGN.md for the design guidelines. Any UI-related change must follow the DESIGN.md guidelines.

Next, you're probably curious what @ actually is. We've used similar syntax before, like "please read @SPEC.md," but it's worth pointing out that it works a little differently depending on where you use it:

  • @ in a conversation: The file only gets read for "this one conversation."
  • @ inside CLAUDE.md: This is CLAUDE.md's import syntax (pull this file in), so the file gets loaded automatically every time you start a new conversation.

With that in mind, let's look at where things stand now. All the core documents are pretty much in place. Did you notice? Here's the role each one plays:

  • SPEC.md: handles "what to build"
  • CLAUDE.md: handles "how to build it"
  • DESIGN.md: handles "what it looks like"

And none of these files disappear when a conversation ends. Every time you start a new conversation, CLAUDE.md automatically pulls in SPEC.md and DESIGN.md, so the spec and design decisions don't get forgotten.

So does it actually lock it in?

DESIGN.md is written, and CLAUDE.md now has @DESIGN.md. But is the style really locked in? I think that's what everyone's wondering, so let's run an experiment and see whether the DESIGN.md guidelines actually keep the style in place.

First, start a brand-new conversation (type /clear), then type the following prompt (don't forget to switch to Plan Mode):

Above the "Add an expense" and "Expense list" headings, please add small section labels: "New entry" and "Recent entries," respectively.

You should then see in the AI's thinking that it really did refer to DESIGN.md. That means the style lock we were hoping for is working.

Wrapping up

That's about it for today. Here are the key points, all wrapped up:

  • UI style evaporates along with the conversation. The fix is to write your design decisions into a DESIGN.md, and you don't have to invent the format yourself. Just use the design.md spec Google Labs open-sourced: YAML holds the exact design tokens, and Markdown holds the design reasoning.
  • Once @DESIGN.md is hooked into CLAUDE.md, every conversation automatically loads the three core documents:
    • SPEC.md handles what to build.
    • CLAUDE.md handles how to build it.
    • DESIGN.md handles what it looks like.

If that all makes sense, see you in the next one.

entry.title: 30 Days of Vibe Coding | Day 16: Making the UI Look Good (Part 1) — The Frontend Design Plugin
entry.content:
Intro

Now that the money-note MVP's core features are done, is the UI just going to stay like this forever?

Of course not. So today we're going to use Anthropic's official Frontend Design plugin to turn the bare-bones screens we built earlier into something more distinctive that looks like a real, production-grade product.

Even Anthropic knows that AI-made UIs tend to look way too plain lol.

Why is AI's default design taste so average?

The biggest problem here is really "what the AI was trained on."

Why does that matter? Because AI learns by training on huge amounts of data, and the screens you're getting right now are basically the "average" of all that training data.

So by default, the AI's best strategy is to give you exactly the kind of screen you're looking at right now.

So how do we fix it? In UI design, there's one thing that matters a lot: "personality" (and no, I don't mean a Quirk from My Hero Academia).

With that in mind, let's keep going!

Installing the Frontend Design plugin

Didn't see that coming, did you? We only just covered /plugin yesterday in the SKILL post, and today we're already putting it to use.

Same as before, type claude to start Claude Code, then type /plugin to open the plugin manager. In the Search field, type frontend-design, and once you find it, click Install.

But let me be a little lazy here and just install it with this command:

/plugin install frontend-design@claude-plugins-official

Before you install it, take a look at the "frontend-design" description:

Create distinctive, production-grade frontend interfaces with high design quality. Generates creative, polished code that avoids generic AI aesthetics.

In short, it's basically...

Build distinctive, product-grade frontend screens and cut down on that generic AI-generated style. Officially certified.

You won't notice any change right after installing it, since it only kicks in when you ask it to work on your UI.

The makeover: talk about the feel, not CSS

Before we start, let's look at the current screen so we can do a Before & After comparison:

This makeover is going to touch a lot of places, since we're basically redoing the whole layout. So I strongly recommend using Plan Mode. That way it lays out the makeover plan first, and you only run it once you've confirmed it looks right.

When describing the UI, you can skip CSS entirely, but you do need to turn that feeling into design constraints you can actually check. That's how Frontend Design can build the screen you have in mind. Here's a prompt I used for reference:

Please call and use the frontend-design skill. First read SPEC.md and get familiar with the current components, then propose a UI update plan.

Product direction: a warm-toned paper ledger. Quiet, clean, numbers first. Not a generic blue-and-white admin dashboard.

Design constraints:
- Page background #F3EFE7, cards #FFFDF8, text #1F2925, secondary text #56625C
- Primary action #245C4A, accent #9A4F20, error #962E2E
- Use the system Traditional Chinese fonts, don't load remote fonts; no gradients, glass effects, emoji icons, or over-the-top shadows
- The home page needs a header area, a summary of this month's total spending and number of entries, tabs, the expense form, and the expense list
- Besides the pie chart, the stats page needs category names, amounts, and percentages as text, not relying on color alone
- Every input, select, and button is at least 44px tall, with visible labels and keyboard focus
- No horizontal scrolling at 375px; at 768px and up, content max width is 780px
- Support prefers-reduced-motion

Boundaries: keep the existing data structures and features. Only adjust markup structure and styles, and don't add any UI libraries.

In the plan, list the files that will change, the purpose of each file, and a review checklist for both features and screens after the changes.

When you're done, tell me which design decisions you made and why.

If you're a total beginner, your first reaction to this prompt is probably:

"Huh? That's way too complicated. How could I ever write something like that?"

I know this prompt looks pretty scary, but if you break it apart, it's really just the answers to these five questions. And I'm sure you can answer all five:

  • What feel do you want? That's the opening line, "a warm-toned paper ledger. Quiet, clean, numbers first." Just describe it the way you would to a friend, like "I want that warm feeling of a handwritten ledger, not something that looks like a company's internal admin system."
  • What absolutely has to be on the screen? Name every "must-have" on the home page and the stats page one by one, so the AI doesn't redesign the important stuff out of existence.
  • What do you hate? This one's actually the most important. The AI's default bundle is gradients, glass effects, over-the-top shadows, and so on. If you don't explicitly say "no," it'll assume you want them.
  • How small a screen does it need to work on? Give it a phone width (375px is roughly the width of an iPhone screen) and basic tappability (buttons shouldn't be too small to hit). Otherwise it'll look great on your computer and break on your phone.
  • What's off-limits? We're just giving the app new clothes, not performing surgery. So be clear that data and features can't be touched, or the screen gets prettier while the expense tracking breaks completely.

"So... what about colors like #245C4A? How am I supposed to know those?"

Honestly, you don't have to write it like I did. You can just tell the AI:

I want the feel of a warm-toned paper ledger. Please give me some color palettes for reference.

That's another technique you can use. In the end, all you need to say is "this is the feel I want" or "this color is too cool-toned, make it a bit warmer," and let the AI pick the rest.

So do you need to really know CSS or design? Basically, no. You just need to answer those five questions, and Frontend Design fills in the rest of the design knowledge.

That doesn't mean you can get away with knowing nothing about CSS or design. You still need some basics, otherwise how would you know whether what the AI made looks good? What I mean is that you can have a shot at a good-looking screen without spending time designing it yourself.

If the Plan Mode plan looks fine, go ahead and run the makeover plan. When it's done, don't forget to ask the AI to start the server so you can take a look. Here's a screenshot of mine after the makeover for reference:

What about the stats page? Of course it got updated too:

Iterating on the details: design by conversation

Even though the updated screens already look way better than before, the first version usually still needs some tweaking. "Taste" is subjective, after all, and there might be a few spots that just bug you, like...

  • Why is this number so small?
  • Why does this button look like that?

That's when you move into the "iterating on the details" stage.

This stage is pretty simple: get the screen to where you're mostly happy with it, then slowly polish the small stuff.

But when you're tweaking, don't just say something vague like "make it more refined," because the AI has no idea what "refined" means to you. Be clear about which element and what you want it to become, like...

Make the "This month's total spending" number a bit bigger. It's the most important information on the whole page.
Keep the current colors for the category tags, don't add any new colors.
Don't change the size of the delete button, just turn it warning red on mouse hover.

Don't dump a whole pile on it at once. When tweaking, usually stick to a few points:

  • Only mention 2–3 things
  • Look at the result first
  • Then decide whether to tweak more

Then keep going until you're happy with it. The process is like going back and forth on revisions with a designer, except this designer won't give you a dramatic, baroque-level eye-roll lol.

But what if something "just looks off somehow," and you can't put your finger on why? There's a trick I want to share that you can try:

Take a screenshot of the screen, hand it back to the AI, and ask it to help analyze it.

When you hand it over, though, you still need to mention a few key points:

This is the current screen. Please review it from a designer's point of view, and analyze it in terms of "Is the important information obvious enough?", "Is the spacing too cramped?", and "Is it easy to tap on a phone?" When you're done, just tell me your suggestions and reasons. Don't rush to change anything.

The prompt above is built on a few key points:

  • First tell it what you want it to do, like "review the screen."
  • Tell it what point of view to analyze from, like "a designer's point of view."
  • Tell it which aspects you want analyzed, like "Is the important information obvious enough?", "Is the spacing too cramped?", and "Is it easy to tap on a phone?"
  • Keep it from being overly helpful and changing the screen right away, since you won't necessarily agree with every suggestion.

The whole process still comes back to "setting design constraints you can check," because you need to know what's off about the screen before you can decide what to change.

Fake. It's all fake.

So once the screens are updated, can you relax? Nope, not yet.

This round of changes actually touched quite a few files, and there's one big principle you have to remember:

Whenever the UI changes, features might break.

Because of that principle, there's one thing you need to have the AI do: regression testing.

What does that mean? It's simple: retest all the original features one more time to make sure nothing got broken by the layout changes.

There are plenty of ways to do it. You can click through everything yourself:

  • Add an expense
  • Enter bad data on purpose
  • Delete one
  • Refresh the page
  • Check that the stats update along with it

Of course, you can also ask the AI to run through all of that for you. This is where you can use Claude in Chrome to have it drive the browser and run the whole set of tests.

Only after everything checks out should you tell the AI something like this and have it commit for you:

Please commit. In the message, say this is a UI improvement and no features changed.

Wrapping up

That's about it for today, so let's wrap up with a few takeaways.

  • AI-made screens look "AI-ish" because when you don't give it a direction, it generates screens based on the average of its training data.
  • Make good use of SKILL extensions, like Frontend Design.
  • Your prompt doesn't need CSS, but you do need to be able to answer these five questions:
    1. What feel do you want
    2. What absolutely has to be on the screen
    3. What do you hate
    4. How small a screen does it need to work on
    5. What's off-limits
  • Be specific when tweaking. If you don't know how to describe it, take a screenshot and ask the AI for suggestions.
  • After a big UI overhaul, you have to do regression testing: run through the features again to make sure nothing got broken.

That's it for today. See you tomorrow!
