entry.title: 30 Days of Vibe Coding | Day 15: What Are Skills? Teaching AI How You Get Things Done
entry.content:
Intro

We've made it to Day 15, which is also the first day of Week 3!

While building the MVP last week, you probably noticed a few problems. For example, you kept saying the same things over and over, like how commit messages should be written.

Sure, CLAUDE.md has some rules in it (the general ones), but there's still stuff that never made it in there. On top of that, CLAUDE.md has a recommended line limit (somewhere around 200–250 lines). Cram all of this in and it gets way too bloated, but repeating it every time is exhausting.

So today we're going to meet something new: the "SKILL."

SKILL: your own personal ability

So what is a SKILL? In short, it's just a folder plus a Markdown file (a plain-text kind of file, like CLAUDE.md).

"That simple?" you might be thinking.

Yep, it really is that simple.

But what it can do is anything but simple, because a SKILL can contain things like:

  • Steps
  • Rules
  • Examples

It can even include ready-made helper code, so you can just use it whenever you need it.

Still hard to see why that's so powerful, right? Let's switch to a more gaming-style way of looking at it. That might make it click.

Say you're playing an RPG. The character you control usually has a bunch of skills, like "Fireball," "Heal," or "Invisibility." Those are the skills you can use in the game.

So when you want to use one of them, you just shout:

"I'm casting Fireball!"

And your character casts it for you.

But why does just saying "I'm casting Fireball!" actually cast it? Normally, to cast a specific skill like "Fireball," your character needs to know how it's cast, the steps, the rules, and so on. If you had to set all that up yourself, you'd probably have to draw a magic circle, gather your magic ingredients, chant the incantation, and so on before the spell goes off. But once it's packaged up as a skill, you might only need to chant and grab your ingredients, skipping the tedious magic-circle part entirely and casting it right away.

Once that makes sense, we can bring the idea back to SKILLs in the AI world (they work just like a game character's skills). You just tell Claude you want to use a certain SKILL, and it'll handle the steps, rules, examples, and everything else that skill needs, so you can get the task done faster and more efficiently.

Is SKILL a Claude-only feature? Nope. Pretty much every AI vendor out there offers SKILLs. But since this series is built around Claude Code, I'll stick to Claude Code's SKILLs. For other vendors, a quick search will usually turn up their setup, and it's all very similar anyway.

So where do SKILLs live? Let's first look at what one looks like.

First, you have a .claude folder. Inside it is a folder called skills, and every SKILL is its own folder with a SKILL.md inside:

.claude/
└── skills/
    └── commit-message/   ← this folder's name is the SKILL's name
        └── SKILL.md

That skills folder can basically live in one of two places:

  • Inside your project: This is a "project SKILL." It travels with the project, so when your team pulls the project, everyone shares it (which also makes it handy for enforcing team rules, like... commit message format).
  • On your computer (that's ~/.claude/skills/, where ~ means your home folder: /Users/your-name on a Mac, C:\Users\your-name on Windows): This is a "personal SKILL." By default it applies to every project you open, but it never gets committed into any project.

And there are two ways to trigger one:

  • You type /folder-name (for the example above, that's /commit-message) to call it up manually.
  • The AI decides on its own whether the current task matches a SKILL's description, and if it does, pulls it out and uses it.

Pretty interesting, right? Let's keep going and see what else SKILLs can do.

There are actually three kinds of SKILLs

By now you should have a basic idea of what a SKILL is. Next I want to break the concept down a bit further.

Because I think SKILLs can be split into three types:

  • Knowledge:
    • These hold rules, conventions, and style, like "how commit messages should be written in this project" or "what are the main Vue 3 syntax patterns?" That sort of thing.
    • This kind of SKILL usually isn't about getting the AI to do something. It's about keeping the AI from using outdated or wrong information. In RPG terms, it's like a passive skill: always on. You don't have to shout or call it, the AI decides on its own and attaches it.
  • Workflow:
    • These hold step-by-step SOPs, like "how to fix a bug" or "what to run before going live." You usually only call this SKILL when you need it to do that thing.
    • You don't want the AI running this whole pile of steps for no reason. After all, a single deploy for a single product might involve a lot of steps. In RPG terms, this is an active skill: you shout the move (that's /name), and only then does the AI cast it for you.
  • Tool:
    • The last kind is a bit special. It includes ready-made code (usually under scripts/). The upside is the AI doesn't have to rewrite it every time, it just runs that code, like "turn CSV data into a chart" or "batch-compress images" (I personally batch-compress images all the time). In RPG terms again, it's like a "magic item with a skill built in": once it's equipped, the AI can use that item's skill directly.

Why split it up this way? It also kind of answers the question of triggering. For a knowledge SKILL, you want the AI to decide by default whether to use it (would you really want to keep typing /please-use-taiwanese-terms all the time?). For a workflow SKILL, you don't want the AI running it on its own (a workflow can involve a lot of steps). That's why there are two ways to trigger them.

Of course, this split isn't something the official docs define (they only distinguish between "reference knowledge" and "task workflows"). It's just that I think splitting it into three makes it easier to know when to use what, and it keeps a SKILL from turning into a mess where everything gets stuffed in.

The complicated relationship between SKILLs and slash commands

Next, let's talk about the complicated relationship between SKILLs and slash commands. If you've been learning Claude Code on your own, you may have come across something called commands. The idea there is "custom slash commands."

In earlier posts we tried built-in slash commands like /rewind, /clear, and /compact. Those are default commands that Claude Code provides, and you can't change them. So to solve that problem (back before SKILLs existed), Claude Code let you define your own commands. These custom slash commands live under .claude/commands/, and they're also .md files, written in Markdown...

Yep, that's right. They're about 87% the same as SKILLs.

So which one should we actually use? Honestly, I'd just tell you to use SKILLs, since they work across different AI vendors (like Codex, Gemini, and so on).

Here's a table to make the relationship between Skills, built-in slash commands, and custom slash commands clear:

Built-in slash commandsCustom slash commands (old)Skills
Examples/help, /clear, /compact.md files in .claude/commands/Folders in .claude/skills/
What it isFeatures hardcoded into Claude CodeCustom prompt templatesA full skill package

How to split the work with CLAUDE.md

Next up is another topic that can get confusing: "Should I write this in CLAUDE.md or in a SKILL?"

It's actually simple. Just remember one line:

One is the constitution, the absolute highest rule. The other is a skill you only use when you need it.

That's also why things were set up the way they were earlier. Every /clear (/new) reloads CLAUDE.md, which is what makes it the "constitution." A skill only gets loaded when you need it (technically the skill's description does get loaded, but not the whole skill package. We'll get to that later). So you only know the skill is called "Fireball," but you don't know how it's cast, the steps, the rules, and so on. All of that only gets loaded when you need it.

This design is also a way to save on Context usage.

Skills you can install: a first look at /plugin

Now that you know the SKILL basics, you probably think we're about to write our own SKILL, right?

Nope. Writing your own SKILL from scratch is a bit too hardcore for now, so first let's try another way: "installing one."

"Huh? Installing one?"

Yep. Basically you use a SKILL someone else already wrote, so you don't have to start from zero.

So open your terminal, type claude to start Claude Code, then type /plugin. You can browse around in Discover:

As an example, let's install the skill-creator SKILL. Once you find it, press the space bar to select it, then press Enter:

Next, I personally recommend installing this SKILL at the "user" level. It's a SKILL for my own use and has nothing to do with any specific project, so I install it for myself instead of just for this project:

In short, the skill-creator SKILL helps you create new SKILLs. If you want to package up your own SKILLs, it's super handy.

If you can't be bothered to hunt for it, you can also just type the command:

/plugin install skill-creator@claude-plugins-official

Once it's installed, don't forget to type /reload-plugins so it takes effect.

You might notice something odd here. We installed a SKILL, but it didn't go under ~/.claude/skills/. It went to ~/.claude/plugins/ instead.

The real difference between those two folders isn't "where things go," it's "who's in charge of managing them."

~/.claude/skills/ is the area you manage by hand. You drop SKILL folders in, update them, and delete them yourself. Claude Code just reads them. It doesn't know or care where those files came from.

But stuff installed from a marketplace is different. Claude Code has to keep records for you: which marketplace a package came from, what version it is, and when it was installed. Only with those records can it check for updates and remove things for you later. So those records and files all get kept under ~/.claude/plugins/, where it manages them itself (if you're curious, open ~/.claude/plugins/installed_plugins.json and you'll see the install records one by one).

It's basically like your phone. Files you copy onto your phone yourself won't get updated by the system. But apps installed from the App Store can be auto-updated and removed with one tap, because the store knows where they came from and what version they are. That's why those apps live somewhere the system manages itself.

There's also a more fundamental reason...

"A plugin is not the same as a skill."

A skill is just one of the things a plugin "might" carry. A plugin can also include custom slash commands (yep, the ones we just talked about) and other more advanced features. So what you're actually installing is "a whole plugin package," and naturally it goes under ~/.claude/plugins/.

And because plugins are managed separately, the skills they bring in get the plugin's name attached when you call them, in the format /plugin-name:skill-name. So you don't have to worry about them clashing with the SKILLs you put in ~/.claude/skills/ yourself.

So how do you know what a plugin will install? Before installing, you can open that plugin's details page. There's a Will install field that tells you what it's going to bring in:

If you can, try to only install plugins from the official marketplace. Official plugins go through review, so they're relatively safer.

Wrapping up

That pretty much covers SKILLs, so let's do a final recap:

  • A SKILL is really just a folder plus a SKILL.md. Put it in a project and it belongs to that project. Put it in ~/.claude/skills/ and it works across all your projects (basically, your whole computer gets it).
  • There are two main ways to trigger one:
    • You call it manually by typing /name.
    • You let the AI decide from the description whether to use it and call it.
  • SKILLs can be split into three kinds:
    1. Knowledge (passive skill, the AI attaches it on its own).
    2. Workflow (active skill, only cast when you shout the move).
    3. Tool (a magic item with a skill built in, comes with code it runs directly).
  • Custom slash commands are about 87% the same as SKILLs, but I'd just go with SKILLs, since they work across different AI tools.
  • CLAUDE.md is the top-level "constitution" that loads every time. A SKILL is a "skill" that only gets loaded when needed. Things you have to follow every time go in the constitution, and things you only use now and then get packaged as a SKILL.
  • SKILLs can be installed (/plugin), but before you install, check what Will install is going to bring in, and stick to the official marketplace as much as possible.
  • There are two ways to get them:
    • SKILLs you write yourself go in ~/.claude/skills/.
    • Installed ones get kept in ~/.claude/plugins/.

If that all makes sense, that's where we'll stop for today.

See you tomorrow.

entry.title: 30 Days of Vibe Coding | Day 14: Week 2 Wrap-Up — Should You Actually Read AI-Written Code?
entry.content:
Intro

Wow! That's Week 2 wrapped up.

Think back to Day 8: all we had was a SPEC.md. Today we have an app that can record expenses, edit and delete them, show stats, and keep your data even after you close and reopen it. Building something simple and usable in a single week is pretty cool, right?

So today we're doing a bit of wrap-up: a full review against SPEC.md, a look back at how the week went, and an answer to the question most people have:

All this code wasn't written by me. Do I still need to read it?

The full MVP review

Back on Day 8 we turned our idea into a spec (SPEC.md), and while planning it, we also set up acceptance criteria. Open SPEC.md and find section 7 and you'll see them:

## 7. Acceptance criteria

Definition of done for v1:

1. Open it on a phone, tap the button in the bottom-right corner → enter 120 → tap "Food" → save. An expense is recorded in three actions
2. The newly recorded entry shows up at the top of the list right away, and this month's total goes up at the same time
3. The pie chart's slice sizes and the breakdown percentages correctly reflect that month's amount for each category
4. Clicking any row in the list lets you edit the amount / category / date / note, and after saving, the list and stats update together
5. Deleting shows a confirmation first, and once confirmed, that entry disappears from both the list and the stats
6. Refresh the page and all the data is still there
7. Switching to a month with no records shows an empty state, not a broken chart
8. Change an entry's date to last month, and it disappears from this month and shows up in last month
9. Press `◀` repeatedly to go back several months, then click "This month" once to return to the current month. The "This month" button then disappears,
   and the left and right arrows in the month switcher don't shift position
10. **After adding an expense and switching to the stats page, total spending, number of entries, and the pie chart all reflect the latest data**
11. Switching months on the stats page swaps all three numbers and the pie chart to that month; switching tabs doesn't reset the month back to this month

You might be thinking the screen doesn't look like much and the features aren't anything special, that kind of thing. But what we're reviewing here is the "core MVP."

So what's a "core MVP"? It's really just the most basic of basic features an expense tracker needs:

  • Add, edit, and delete expenses
  • Switch months and see the breakdown by category
  • Save data (it's still there after you close and reopen)

These are the most basic features of any expense tracker. Without them, it doesn't count as "a usable expense tracker," which is why I'm defining this as the "core MVP."

But this core MVP doesn't mean the journey ends here. Later on we'll add things like visual guidelines so the whole thing looks more like a product. We'll fill those in over the next two weeks.

Look at your week: git log is your progress bar

Type this into your terminal:

git log --oneline

The screenshot here is just an example, not the actual output from your project. Run git log --oneline in your own project and take a look.

Of course, you can also just have the AI run it for you.

With Git, you can see the whole trail of your Vibe Coding. As the project grows, that trail gets more and more valuable (when something goes wrong, you can go back to a commit and start over from there, or pull the code from a commit and use it as an example). That's why every commit needs a clear message. Otherwise it's not much use.

The big question: should you read AI-written code?

I think it's about time to answer the question "should you read the code AI writes?" After the past few days, a lot of you are probably pretty confused about this.

I'll just give you the conclusion straight up:

Yes, but "reading" it doesn't mean going through it line by line, word by word.

After all, you might not even know syntax like computed, console.log, or ref. Making you read it line by line would be pure torture. But if I told you that you could skip it entirely, that wouldn't be right either. That's like driving a car with no dashboard: you have no idea how much gas is in the tank or how fast you're going. Then a cop pulls you over and asks, "Do you know how fast you were going?" and you can't even answer a basic question like that.

So what I mean by "reading" here is that you can at least explain in plain language what the code is doing, like...

  • Where the data is stored
  • What its format looks like
  • Which files it passes through between the user tapping "add an expense" and the screen updating

These are all things you can understand. Nobody's asking you to understand every detail and every word of how the code is implemented.

So... which parts do you need to be able to explain, and which can you let slide?

I split it with two questions:

  1. If this code (feature) is wrong, does it hurt?
  2. Can you understand it?

Those two questions happen to make four quadrants:

Can understandCan't understand
Hurts if wrong (wrong amounts, lost data, deleting what shouldn't be deleted)Read it yourself once. For example: how the money is calculated, how discounts are applied.Have the AI explain it, until you understand. For example: where's the data stored? How is it saved and read?
Doesn't hurt if wrong (ugly, misaligned, odd wording)A quick skim is enough. For example: button labels, wording of messages, colorsDon't bother reading it, leave it to tests and Code Review later. For example: style settings, library initialization, config files, etc.

When you're just starting out with Vibe Coding, most of your code will be in the two boxes on the right (the "can't understand" column). So:

  • For what hurts if it's wrong, have it explain it to you until you understand.
  • For what doesn't hurt if it's wrong, let it go for now, since you can have the AI help adjust it later anyway.

Over time, as you keep iterating, your knowledge and understanding will slowly move toward the left column (can understand), so there's no need to worry too much at the start.

The line between "hurts" and "doesn't hurt" shifts depending on the size of the project. If you just want to quickly test an idea and throw it away when you're done, you don't need to worry too much. But if it's something you'll keep using and open up to other people, or you want to learn from it, that bar goes up a lot.

Week 2 hands-on checklist

To close out Week 2, here's a hands-on checklist for you to go through:

  • Every core acceptance criterion in SPEC.md passes, and the MVP runs.
  • git log shows the week's commit trail.
  • You can explain in plain language where your expense data is stored.
  • You've gone through each of these at least once: sending a plan back, and reporting a bug with the debugging trio.
  • npm run build succeeds (you can also have the AI run it for you).

Wrapping up

That's about it for time. That's a wrap on Week 2.

In one week we quickly turned a SPEC.md into a usable MVP. The screen is still pretty bare-bones, but at least it's feature-complete. Here's what we got done this week:

  • Got the workflow running smoothly:
    • From spec → laying the groundwork → planning → small-step feature iteration → setting up a debugging workflow → running the review, with a commit at every step.
  • You don't need to read the code line by line, but you should at least know what it's doing.

I hope this post helped. See you in the next one.

entry.title: 30 Days of Vibe Coding | Day 13: Bringing the Numbers to Life — A Stats Page and Pie Chart with Chart.js
entry.content:
Intro

Our expense tracker app pretty much has a working prototype now. There's even a category breakdown in there that shows you which categories you're spending the most on.

But... humans are visual creatures. If the screen looks nice and has charts, that beats showing a pile of numbers. So in this post I'll show you how to build a stats page that brings those boring line-by-line numbers to life.

At the same time, we'll cover how to deal with tech you're not familiar with, like how to choose and set up something like Chart.js.

Ask the AI to recommend a dish

So what do you do when you're facing tech you don't know? Let me use eating at a restaurant as an example.

Say we walk into a restaurant and the menu has a ton of dishes, but we're not sure what to order. So we ask the server to recommend a few. That's exactly what we're doing here too.

When you need to build something you're not familiar with, you can ask the AI to recommend a few options and list the pros and cons, and then you make the final call on which tech to use.

So... how do you do it? Here's an example prompt I put together for you (don't forget to switch to Plan Mode):

I want to build a stats page that shows this month's spending stats:
- Add two tabs to the app: Expenses (the current screen) and Stats.
- The stats page shows this month's total spending, this month's number of entries, and a pie chart of this month's breakdown by category.
- Next to the pie chart, also list the category name, amount, and percentage. The data can't rely on color alone.
- Please pull the stats calculation logic out into pure functions. Don't tie it to the UI or storage.
- Acceptance criteria: after adding an expense and switching to the stats page, the total and the pie chart should both reflect the latest data.

On the tech side, you can read SPEC.md to understand my current project's tech. After reading it, list two or three chart library options commonly used in the Vue ecosystem, with the pros and cons of each. Check the options with me first, and only write the plan after I've decided.
Consideration: this project is small. I want the simplest thing that's good enough. No overkill.

This prompt is a little longer than the past few days. The first half is the feature requirements and acceptance criteria, and only the second half is the ordering:

  1. Have it recommend first
  2. I make the call.

The reason you have to state all the requirements at once is that once the plan comes out and you approve it, it'll build the whole thing in one go. There won't be a break in the middle for you to add more requirements.

You should see the AI recommend a few mainstream libraries like Chart.js or ECharts:

Even though Chart.js + vue-chartjs isn't the recommended option, I'd still personally pick it. After all, it says right there that it's "the most mainstream in the Vue ecosystem, with the most docs and examples, and pie charts are a built-in type." Its API is simple too, which makes it the best fit for a small project.

At this point, please don't rush to press "Yes, and use auto mode." Read through it properly first!

Whenever there's something you don't understand, feel free to press ESC or ask the AI to explain it in "Tell Claude what to change." That way you'll understand its approach better, which will also help you with future development.

Getting to work

Once you've picked, it'll start writing the plan. Same as before, you don't need to read every word. Just look at a few key points:

  • Is the library it's using the one you just picked?
  • Did it pull the "calculation" part out into pure functions like you asked, instead of stuffing everything into the component?
  • Did SPEC.md get updated too? For example, my SPEC.md originally said not to install a chart library. Now that we've decided to install one, that line needs to change as well.

Here's my full plan for reference.

By the way, my plan also made a decision I didn't ask for: it removed the row of category breakdown bars from the expenses page and moved it to the stats page. Its reasoning was that the same data shouldn't be drawn two different ways, because if you change one, it's easy to forget the other. So when it's done, you'll notice the bars on the home page are gone. Don't assume it broke something. For decisions like this that it adds on its own, approve them if you understand the reasoning, and ask if you don't. Don't just quietly let them through.

If it all looks fine, press "Yes, and use auto mode". It'll run the install first (if a permission prompt pops up, give it a quick look before approving), and then build.

One more reminder: package versions are usually the thing the AI's memory is most likely to have out of date. So once it finishes installing, I recommend checking the version numbers in package.json to make sure they're the latest, or the version you want.

Then you'll see it create two pieces:

  • A file that handles the "calculating" (for me it's src/utils/stats.js)
  • A chart component that handles the "drawing" (src/components/CategoryPieChart.vue)

Your file names might not be exactly the same as mine, but you don't need to understand the code. Just know how the work is split: the first one only calculates "how much was spent in each category and what share each one takes." It takes data in and spits numbers out, and doesn't care about the screen at all. The second one takes those numbers and draws the pie chart.

If you want to check that it did this, just open the project folder and see whether two similar files showed up.

If you're really curious what's going on inside, just ask it "Explain in plain language what stats.js does." That's way faster than forcing yourself to read the code.

Review: does the chart move with the data?

Next, of course, we need to review the result. Seeing the screen below doesn't mean it passed:

So how do we actually review this? First, let's clear out the practice data from before:

  • Open the developer tools (F12, or Cmd+Option+I on macOS)
  • Switch to the Application tab, and under Local Storage on the left, find your URL (normally http://localhost:5173)
  • Delete the money-note:records:v1 key, then refresh the page.

The screen should be empty now. Next, let's add some test data:

  1. Add Food 120 for this month
  2. Add Transport 80 for this month
  3. Add Entertainment 999 for last month
  4. Switch to the stats page

Here's what we expect:

  1. This month's total is 200, with 2 entries
  2. Food 60%
  3. Transport 40%
  4. Last month's 999 isn't counted at all

Once that checks out, go back to the expenses page and add one more entry, "Entertainment 200 for this month," then switch back to the stats page. This time, we expect:

  1. This month's total is 400, with 3 entries
  2. Food 30%
  3. Transport 20%
  4. Entertainment 50%

And with that, we've finished Week 2's core MVP. Don't forget to have the AI commit.

Wrapping up

So the stats page is done too. Let's wrap up with a quick summary:

  • When you run into tech you don't know, ask the AI to recommend a dish: give it your requirements and constraints, have it list options with pros and cons, and only say yes once you understand the reasoning. You don't have to pick the one it marked as recommended.
  • Once you approve a Plan Mode plan, it builds the whole thing in one go, so state all your requirements at once. For decisions it adds to the plan on its own, approve them if you understand the reasoning, and ask if you don't.
  • After installing packages, take a look at the versions in package.json. Don't trust the AI's memory.
  • Review by the numbers, not the chart: use a fixed set of entries, work out the expected values ahead of time, and compare. The chart looking like "it kind of changed" doesn't count.

As of today, all the core features in SPEC.md are in place, and this expense tracker app is basically a usable MVP.

See you tomorrow.

entry.title: 30 Days of Vibe Coding | Day 12: Something Broke?! A Debugging Workflow for Vibe Coding
entry.content:
Intro

In the last post we went through three rounds of feature work, and we also left a bug in on purpose: the index delete bug.

So today we're talking about the Vibe Coding debugging workflow: from spotting a bug, to guiding the AI to fix it, to regression-testing it and committing.

Of course, you might be thinking: AI is so smart these days, how would we even run into bugs?

Actually, you'd be wrong. No matter how smart or capable the AI is, if you don't review its work and don't try to understand it, you're going to run into exactly this.

Hold on a sec!

Before we start, I'd like you to install a Chrome extension called Claude in Chrome.

Why do you need it? In short...

It lets Claude Code operate your browser directly, so it can do the debugging itself instead of you describing everything to it.

With this extension, you can even have Claude Code pull emails from Gmail, grab data from web pages, or even operate your project for you. These are all things Claude Code can do.

Once it's installed, let's keep going.

The worst way to report a bug

First, I want to talk about the bug reports I run into most often in my own dev work. They usually look like this:

  • "Delete is broken."
  • "The screen won't move."
  • "I clicked the button and nothing happened."

When I get one of these, as an engineer, a few thoughts flash through my head right away:

  • What exactly is broken about delete?
  • What do you mean the screen won't move? It won't update, or it won't navigate?
  • Did nothing happen because you didn't fill in a field so the button was disabled, or did it really do nothing?

Then I try it myself and it works fine, so I go dig through the code looking for clues. When I still can't find anything, all I can do is tell the person who reported it: "It works fine on my end, can you try again?" And then we go back and forth like that a bunch of times.

The same thing applies to AI. The AI also needs enough information from you to fix the problem. If you don't give it enough, it's stuck doing what a human engineer would do: wildly guessing at possible causes and reading tons of code (burning through a lot of Tokens). Then you start complaining that the AI is dumb and slow, when really the root cause is that "you never described the problem clearly in the first place."

It has no way of knowing what you did, what the flow was, what you saw, or what you expected. So it guesses blindly and forces a change, and you end up spending a lot of time verifying it over and over.

At that point, how is that any different from playing Minesweeper?

So next I'm going to give you a formula and a workflow, so you can explain things to the AI precisely, verify the fix, and get bugs fixed fast.

The debugging trio: reproduce, expected, actual

I break debugging down into three main steps:

  1. Steps to reproduce: what you did that made the bug happen
  2. Expected result: what you expected to happen
  3. Actual result: what actually happened

Is that all? Nope. You should also attach screenshots or a screen recording whenever you can.

AI can read images directly these days. Pair them with a text description and it can understand your problem much more precisely.

Now that you know the debugging trio, let's apply it to the delete bug we left behind yesterday:

There's a bug in the delete feature. Steps to reproduce:
1. Starting with no data, add yesterday's lunch for 120, category Food
2. Then add today's drink for 60, category Food
3. The list is sorted newest to oldest:
  - Today's drink
  - Yesterday's lunch
4. I click the "lunch" entry to open the edit form, then I just press delete and confirm

Expected result: the lunch entry disappears
Actual result: lunch is still there, and the "drink" entry is the one that disappeared

I didn't see any error messages during this. Please analyze it and tell me what you think the cause is.

There's actually one part of the flow I deliberately left out: what you see after "opening the edit form." That's to simulate something users still miss all the time when they report problems. If you look closely, you'll notice the data that actually gets loaded into the form is the "drink" entry's data, not lunch.

Here too, I recommend using Plan Mode so the AI can properly analyze things and find the problem.

Pretty interesting, right? I even turn on Plan Mode for debugging. After all the feature work so far, you might have gotten the impression that Plan Mode is only for building features. Not really. Plan Mode works for debugging too, because it analyzes the problem and gives you a suggested direction for the fix, so you're on much firmer ground.

If it all looks fine, same as before, press "Yes, and use auto mode" and the AI will start fixing the problem for you.

Also, did you notice that in this diagnosis it mentions "this bug was left in on purpose"? That's the payoff from Day 10, when we had it save plans into docs/plans/. Yesterday's plan is sitting right there in docs/plans/03-edit-and-delete.md, so it can look up how that decision was made on its own. You don't have to explain it again.

If you notice it didn't go looking on its own, you can just tell it "Please read docs/plans/03-edit-and-delete.md first." Still, having a record of what you did before is way faster than explaining it all over again.

All of this really comes down to building a habit: describe the problem clearly so the AI can understand what you ran into. That goes for human engineers and AI alike. And this whole exercise happens to prove one thing at the same time:

Just because you reviewed it doesn't mean there are no bugs. It just means the scenarios you tested happened not to have any.

That's exactly why so many engineers ask you for more information. So stop blaming engineers for being slow at debugging.

After all, if you never described the problem clearly, how are they supposed to be fast?

Where to look for clues: the console or a screenshot

A lot of the time, a bug doesn't show up on the screen at all. So what do you do then?

First you need to be clear about what you're building, since different kinds of projects have different ways of handling this. Our practice expense tracker app is a Web App, so we can open the browser's developer tools and check the error messages in the Console. Those messages usually tell you what's wrong. Opening it is easy:

  • Windows / Linux: F12
  • macOS: Cmd + Option + I

Then just switch to the "Console" tab and you'll see the error messages.

Handling them is simple too: copy the whole thing and paste it to the AI. Don't translate it, summarize it, or come up with your own explanation, because the parts you think don't matter are often the key. Just handing it straight to the AI is the fastest way.

Some of the errors in the screenshot above come from browser extensions. So if you see a lot of red text in the console, try turning your extensions off and testing again (or use an incognito window). That helps you avoid chasing the wrong thing.

Next up is the second kind: bugs that are hard to describe in words (layout out of whack, wrong colors, inconsistent text sizes, and so on). For these, I recommend taking a screenshot, dragging it straight into the AI's input box, and then following the same debugging workflow. That saves you a lot of time writing descriptions.

Of course, if you can describe it clearly, that's still best.

The fix isn't the end: regression-test it the same way

No matter what, when the AI tells you it's fixed it, everything's fine, or it's all done, that doesn't mean you're off the hook. It just means it's handing things back to you, because you're the owner of this project.

When you review, take out those same steps to reproduce and walk through them again yourself:

There's a bug in the delete feature. Steps to reproduce:
1. Starting with no data, add yesterday's lunch for 120, category Food
2. Then add today's drink for 60, category Food
3. The list is sorted newest to oldest:
  - Today's drink
  - Yesterday's lunch
4. I click the "lunch" entry to open the edit form, then I just press delete and confirm

Expected result this time: the edit form shows lunch's 120, and after deleting, lunch disappears and the drink is still there.

Check it again by following the exact steps you originally reported to the AI. You do want to know whether it actually fixed the bug you gave it, right? Don't just call it done because the AI said it's fixed.

On top of that, you also need to check that the old features didn't break, since the part that just changed might affect other places. So this is when you go through the old features too and make sure they still work.

Remember a few ground rules:

  • The AI saying "I fixed it" doesn't count. It only counts once you've checked it yourself.
  • Whether old features got broken is also something you have to confirm yourself.

Only when all of that checks out is it actually "fixed." At this point you can tell the AI:

I've reviewed it. The original bug is gone, the old features aren't broken, and the known TODOs are all gone. Please commit.

And with that, you've gone through one full round of the Vibe Coding debugging workflow. The same workflow applies whether you're working with human engineers or AI.

When it just won't get fixed: three fallbacks

Next I want to share a scenario people don't talk about much: when you've gone back and forth several times and the AI still can't fix it.

In that situation, doing nothing isn't an option. Instead, you should have a few fallbacks ready. Here are three you can use:

  1. Ask from a different angle: Don't keep repeating useless descriptions like "it's still broken." Try it a few more times and give the AI what you newly noticed, for example... "deleting the first entry works, deleting the second one goes wrong." Sometimes a new clue helps find the problem.
  2. Narrow it down: First have the AI verify the data flow. Tell it to ignore the screen for now and show you the data before and after the delete. Split the problem into data and screen. The screen is usually driven by the data, so the screen only means something once you've confirmed the data is right.
  3. Restore a single file with git: After going back and forth with the AI several times, ask it to restore things to the last commit. Every feature commit you made was saved for exactly this moment. Have the AI list which files were changed first, look them over before you say yes, and only restore the one file that's broken, instead of wiping out all the progress you worked hard on today.

All three fallbacks are telling you one thing:

AI doesn't nail every bug fix or feature on the first try. The people who plan their fallbacks are the ones who go the distance.

So, putting the whole thing together, the workflow looks like this:

flowchart TD
    A["Spot a bug"] --> B["Debugging trio<br>steps to reproduce, expected, actual"]
    B --> C{"Any error messages?"}
    C -->|"Yes"| D["Paste the red console text straight to the AI"]
    C -->|"No"| E["Add one line: no error messages seen"]
    D --> F["Turn on Plan Mode<br>let it diagnose first, approve after reading the plan"]
    E --> F
    F --> G{"Regression test<br>original bug gone and old features not broken?"}
    G -->|"Pass"| H["Commit, with the cause in the message"]
    G -->|"Stuck three rounds with no progress"| I["Ask from a different angle / narrow it down / have AI restore a single file"]
    I --> B

Wrapping up

By now you should have a pretty good handle on the debugging process, so let's wrap up with a quick summary.

When you're Vibe Coding, don't panic when you hit a problem. Follow this workflow:

  • Describe it with the debugging trio: steps to reproduce, expected, actual. If there's red text, paste all of it; if it's a visual problem, send a screenshot.
  • Turn on Plan Mode and let it diagnose the problem before it touches anything.
  • Review the fix yourself: the original bug is really gone and no old features got broken. Only commit once it passes.
  • If it won't get fixed, use the three fallbacks: ask from a different angle, narrow it down, and restore only the specific file.

Tomorrow we'll do something more fun: let the numbers do the talking by adding a stats page and a pie chart to the app.

Hopefully this post makes fixing bugs feel a little less like a lottery. See you tomorrow on Day 13.

entry.title: 30 Days of Vibe Coding | Day 11: One Feature at a Time — How to Split Your Prompts
entry.content:
Intro

Yesterday we finally finished our first feature: "add an expense."

But... is that it? Nope. Next we're going to iterate on features and have the AI finish off the rest for us.

Sure, you could do it in one line: "Please read @SPEC.md and build all the remaining features."

But I really don't recommend that. It makes it easy to lose track of what it changed, and when something breaks, it's hard to trace and debug. You end up spending way more energy hunting down problems instead of focusing on building features.

So today's focus isn't really the features themselves. It's splitting the build into three rounds, with each round getting a clear prompt that tells the AI exactly how to build something that fits what you need.

Three parts of a good prompt

Personally, I think a good feature prompt has three parts:

  1. Current state: clearly describe what's on the screen right now and which part you want to change this time.
  2. What you want: what's the goal this round, and what are the specific fields and behaviors?
  3. Acceptance criteria: how do you know it's done right?

It might be a little hard at first to see why these three parts make for good feature work. Basically, all three are there to prevent one thing:

Stopping the AI from filling in too many blanks on its own, so its idea doesn't drift too far from yours.

AI is really smart these days, but sometimes it's a little too clever for its own good. So you have to describe what you want clearly, and then the AI can build something that actually fits.

There's one more thing I want to point out, and it's about "current state."

Current state just means describing what you can see and what's happening right now, like...

  • Something on the screen looks off.
  • A button doesn't do anything when you click it.

You don't need to go dig up which folder the code lives in or what the file is called. That's not the Vibe Coding spirit at all — your job is to guide the AI toward the feature you want.

For the AI, the project is right in front of it. It'll read it on its own, and it'll find the file even if you can't name it. The real problem is the other way around:

It can't see the picture in your head. That's the part worth spending your effort describing.

With that out of the way, let's see these three parts in action.

Round one: category breakdown

First, build a good habit: whenever you start a "new feature," type /clear so you're working on a clean desk. That keeps earlier discussions and build steps from affecting this round. That influence is what we call "noise."

Once the desk is clean, we're ready for the first round.

After yesterday's "add an expense," the home page already shows this month's total and a list of this month's entries, so you know how much you've spent this month:

But an expense tracker can't be that bare-bones, right? A total and a list alone still don't make it easy to see where the money actually went. So next we're building a "category breakdown," so users can see clearly which categories their money goes to.

We're going to build the "category breakdown" from SPEC.md. Here's how I'd write the prompt (don't forget to turn on Plan Mode before sending it):

The home page currently shows this month's total and this month's entries, but I can't tell which category I'm spending the most on.

Please read the "Category breakdown" part of section 5.1 in SPEC.md and build it. For placement, refer to the wireframe near the top of SPEC.md (below the total, above the list).

Acceptance criteria:

1. If this month I record Food 120, Food 80, and Transport 100, the screen should show two horizontal bars: Food $200 on top, Transport $100 below, with the Food bar longer
2. Categories with no spending this month shouldn't show up — no row of zeros
3. Round percentages to whole numbers. If three categories each have 100, show 33%, 33%, 33%. Adding up to 99% is fine, don't force it to 100%
4. Last month's data isn't included in the calculation

That prompt is really just the three parts:

  1. Current state: the home page has this month's total and entries, but I can't tell which category I'm spending the most on.
  2. What you want: add a row of category breakdown bars below the total.
  3. Acceptance criteria: four checks.

Notice I never said "please change this file or that component." We let the AI figure that out. What matters is telling it what you want the screen to look like. And if there's anything it's not sure about (like styling), it'll still ask you:

The Plan Mode plan is long, but you don't need to read every word. Just focus on three things:

  • Which files is it going to touch?
  • What's it not doing?
  • What are the acceptance criteria?

The rest? Skim it so you get the general idea.

If it all looks fine, go ahead and click "Yes, and use auto mode" and let it get to work.

You'll notice that after you approve it, it doesn't start changing code right away. It first produces docs/plans/02-category-breakdown.md. That's the rule we added to CLAUDE.md yesterday kicking in, so from today on you don't need to remind it anymore.

And finally, there's our category breakdown, built and working:

Round two: edit and delete (with a bug left in on purpose)

With the category breakdown done, round two is editing and deleting entries. Sometimes we log the wrong thing or type the wrong amount, so this one really matters.

By now you should know what to do before starting the next round: type /clear first so you have a clean desk.

Then switch to Plan Mode and try something like this prompt for round two:

Right now, clicking an item in the list on the home page does nothing. Please read "Transaction list" in section 5.1 and "Delete" in section 5.3 of SPEC.md.

When the user clicks any item in the list, open an edit form. The form shows four fields, pre-filled with that item's existing data. When the user finishes editing and clicks save, the form closes. The edit form also needs a "Delete" button; clicking it shows a confirmation prompt, and once the user confirms, that item is deleted and the form closes.

One more thing: I want you to deliberately set up a controlled debugging exercise. On purpose, use "which position this item is in the list on screen" to identify the item for editing and deleting — don't use each item's id. Add the comment "TODO for later practice: switch to id" next to the related code, and don't fix it to use id yet.

Acceptance criteria: add three expenses on the same day in a row. Clicking the middle one opens the edit form, clicking delete shows a delete confirmation, and after a successful delete the form closes and only the middle item disappears from the home page list. If you click cancel, nothing changes.

Along the way, it'll probably ask you how to build the popup:

Same as before, you can just go with "recommended" unless you have other ideas.

I need to explain something here. Normally, deleting by index isn't a good approach. This is a known bug I designed on purpose — the right way is to use an id (a unique value). The AI would normally fix this on its own, which is why we have to specifically tell it to make the mistake.

If the difference between index and id doesn't quite click, here's an example: say there are 30 students in a class, and you take attendance by "the Nth student." If they secretly swap seats, you'll have a hard time calling the right person. Think of an id as the student's ID number or name — even if they swap seats, you'll still get the right person.

Once that makes sense, you should get this Plan Mode plan. Same deal: if it looks fine, click "Yes, and use auto mode" and let the AI build it.

Why set up a scenario like this? You're probably wondering. It's to let you experience one thing for yourself:

Passing review doesn't mean there are no bugs. It just means you didn't happen to test that scenario.

After the AI finishes, tell it:

Please commit the current progress with the message: "Practice: edit and delete, index bug left in"

That way, when you (or the AI) go bug hunting later, you'll know this version has a bug in it.

You might have noticed this message doesn't follow the "Feature name: short description" format we set in CLAUDE.md. That's on purpose. Starting it with "Practice:" means you can spot this teaching landmine in the git history at a glance, and it won't get mixed up with normal feature commits.

Round three: switching months

Round three works pretty much the same as the first two. /clear first, switch to Plan Mode, then try something like this prompt:

The top of the home page is currently stuck on this month, and there's no way to see other months' data.

Please read "Month switching" in section 5.1 of SPEC.md. Add an arrow on each side of the year/month line to switch to the previous/next month, plus a "This month" button to jump straight back.

Acceptance criteria: press the left arrow repeatedly to go back three months, and the total, category breakdown, and list should all switch to that month's data. Then click "This month" once to go straight back to the current month. After coming back, the "This month" button disappears, but the left and right arrows don't shift position because of it.

The process is pretty much the same as the first two rounds, so I won't repeat it.

After finishing month switching, these three rounds should leave you with a pretty strong feel for why "one feature at a time" works so well.

flowchart LR
    A["/clear to start a new conversation"] --> B["Switch to Plan Mode"]
    B --> C["Prompt with three parts<br>current state, what you want, acceptance criteria"]
    C --> D["Read the plan, approve only if it looks right"]
    D --> E["AI Agent builds the feature"]
    E --> F{"Review against acceptance criteria"}
    F -->|"Pass"| G["Commit to save"]
    F -->|"Fail"| H["Describe the gap/problem, ask AI to fix it"]
    H --> E
    G --> A

Why type /clear every time?

Across these three rounds, I kept stressing that you should /clear first.

That ties back to the Context Window idea from Day 6 (a desk with limited space). Whatever the AI Agent built earlier (the Context) can pollute what comes next. So usually, every time we start a new round of work, we /clear once so the previous round doesn't affect the current one.

So does our project's shared understanding get wiped? Nope.

When you run /clear, the AI does clean off its desk, but it also puts CLAUDE.md back on it. Then when you start the next round, it works from what's in CLAUDE.md (and pulls in SPEC.md too), so the previous round doesn't bleed into the current one.

So you can use /clear with total peace of mind.

Just to be clear, "one feature at a time" doesn't mean chopping features up as fine as pickles. Aim for a size you can "finish in one go and review at a glance." The category breakdown is one round, edit and delete is one round, but "the color of the delete button" doesn't need its own round — just handle it as part of that round.

If you've been following along exactly, your git history should now have a "Practice: edit and delete, index bug left in" commit. That's the only landmine in the whole series that gets to survive overnight. Tomorrow we'll set it off and then fix it.

Wrapping up

We've finally made it to Day 11. Today we ran three rounds of feature work, all using the same approach:

  1. /clear to clean the desk (start a new conversation), switch to Plan Mode, describe what you need using the three prompt parts (current state, what you want, acceptance criteria), read the plan before approving, review against the criteria when it's done, and commit once it passes.
  2. Start every round in Plan Mode. The plans might be long, but as the project's foundation gets more solid, there's less and less you need to read.
  3. Don't be afraid of /clear wiping important info. Every clear puts CLAUDE.md back in, and the shared understanding that really needs to stick around is already written into SPEC.md and CLAUDE.md.

At this point we've finished all six items on the "In" list in section 3 of SPEC.md. The expense tracker app can now "add, edit, delete, and switch months," and the data gets saved.

But there's still that landmine we planted in the project. Tomorrow we'll walk through a full bug-fixing session live, so hold off on sneaking in a fix before then.
